articles.title: President Akane concludes official visit to Japan
articles.description: Between 24 and 26 November 2026, the President of the Court, Judge Tomoko Akane, held several high-level meetings in Tokyo, Japan.On 24 November 2026, the President was received by H.E. Ms Sanae Takaichi, the Prime Minister of Japan, in order to discuss Japan’s support for the Court and other matters of mutual concern.Following the meeting, President Akane said, “It was truly an honour to speak with Prime Minister Takaichi. Japan has always been amongst the most staunch supporters of the rule of law and international tribunals, including the ICC. Her decision to pay Japan’s 2027 contributions by the end of this year is yet another illustration of Prime Minister Takaichi’s unwavering commitment towards the protection of the International Criminal Court and the values upon which the Court stands. I am truly grateful for Prime Minister Takaichi’s leadership, and I look forward to continuing to work together for our common cause.”During the visit, the President also held meetings with the Minister for Foreign Affairs, H.E. Mr Toshimitsu Motegi, the Minister of Justice, H.E. Mr Takashi Yamashita, and the Prosecutor-General, H.E. Mr Ryuji Kawahara. The President discussed cooperation with the respective offices as well as their shared commitment to maintaining and strengthening the rule of law.On 26 November 2026, the President attended a roundtable on the ICC hosted by the Ambassador of the Netherlands to Japan, H.E. Mr Gilles Beschoor Plug, which brought together representatives of States Parties and Members of Parliament. For further information, please contact the ICC Public Affairs Unit: PublicAffairs.Unit@icc-cpi.int . You can also follow the Court’s activities on Twitter/X, Facebook, YouTube, Instagram and Flickr.

articles.title: Laws of Yesterday’s Wars
articles.description: Laws of Yesterday's wars Volume 5 focuses on Asia and how it organized the chaos and violence of war into “some form of order.”
paragraphs: When Friedrich de Martens wrote in 1879 that international law ceased to operate in Asia and instead became “natural law,” he reflected a view that shaped generations of scholarship. International law was presented as something Europe created and exported. Asia, by contrast, appeared largely as the recipient of European legal ideas rather than a contributor to them. The history tells a different story.

Long before the adoption of the Hague Conventions or the Geneva Conventions, Asian societies had already developed sophisticated ways of regulating violence. It is something I have explored sporadically throughout the Laws of Yesterday’s Wars series, as well as singularly in a forthcoming work called Peace Beyond Westphalia. It came to the fore during my role at the National University of Singapore’s Centre for International Law and, once I started looking, I have found it everywhere. When discussing regional solutions to contemporary conflicts (such as the Thai-Cambodia border last year, all the way through to Konfrontasi) it will almost always be alongside the observation that non-interference is the ASEAN way.

But where does that come from? How are we to interpret the laws of war today with the laws of yesterday’s wars and their specific cultural, geographical, social and religious limbs? Volume 5 of the series sought to collate some of those answers, and this post highlights these contributions.

To write about “Asia” is to wrestle with a conceptual fiction. I therefore approached Volume 5 with the idea of “interpolity.” Interpolity law is a more useful term than “international law” in historical contexts. Interpolity “recognizes the legal character of relations among a range of political communities, including empires, micro-States, and corporate communities such as merchant diasporas, trading companies, and municipalities.”

We see that interpolity tension playing out today in the Indo-Pacific, just as it has for centuries. Recent research identifies interpolity zones as regions marked by “interpenetrating power and weak or uneven claims to territorial sovereignty.” The South China Seas are one such example. The Strait of Johor is another. It is no surprise that the legal concept of adat has flowed through it. Chapters in Volume 5 examine adat in contexts of the Malay peninsula, West Sumatra, and Central Asia. In an earlier volume, adat was examined in the context of Iban of Borneo.

Asian societies modified, re-interpreted, and amended a dat through the cultural lenses they perceived it. This volume went beyond Southeast Asia though. It sought to canvas as wide a spectrum as possible, and rise to the challenge that Jean Pictet posited half a century ago to examine the “pure substance” that “is the heritage of all mankind.”

I deliberately instructed the chapter authors to avoid searching for Asian equivalents of the Geneva Conventions, or measuring historical practices against European models of international humanitarian law (IHL). That would misunderstand both history and law. Instead, the contributors were invited to examine societies on their own terms.
articles.lede: Laws of Yesterday's wars Volume 5 focuses on Asia and how it organized the chaos and violence of war into “some form of order.”

articles.title: Keio University, in collaboration with the ICC, holds the Second Forum of the Asia-Pacific Academic Network (APN) for International Criminal Justice in Tokyo
articles.description: On 26 and 27 November 2026, Keio University, in collaboration with the International Criminal Court (ICC), held the Second Forum of the Asia-Pacific Academic Network for International Criminal Justice (APN) at Keio’s Mita Campus in Tokyo, Japan. Under the theme “Challenges for International Criminal Justice in Asia and Beyond”, the Forum brought together representatives from leading universities across the Asia-Pacific region that have established formal partnerships with the ICC through memoranda of understanding. The discussions focused on opportunities for future academic cooperation, encouraging dialogue on issues related to the Court's mandate, fostering deeper engagement with the ICC and within the APN, and strengthening regional collaboration in support of international justice. The Forum opened with a public session featuring opening remarks by Prof. Kohei Itoh, President of Keio University; Prof. Gentaro Kamei, Dean of the Faculty of Law, Keio University; H.E. Mr Giorgio Aliberti, Ambassador-designate of the European Union to Japan; H.E. Mr Gilles Beschoor Plug, Ambassador of the Kingdom of the Netherlands to Japan; and Ms. Yoko Kamikawa, Member of the House of Representatives of Japan and former Foreign and Justice Minister.In her keynote lecture, ICC President Judge Tomoko Akane addressed the historical significance of the Rome Statute and the ownership that each person must have in the wake of current challenges. She stated “The Rome Statute speaks of the responsibility we bear towards future generations. That responsibility belongs not only to the States that negotiated it, nor to the people who work at the Court. It belongs to all of us. The future of international justice is not something that will simply happen to us. It is something we must collectively choose to build with our own hands.”In his opening remarks, President Itoh underscored the vital role of academia, stating, “At a time when international justice and its institutions face serious challenges, the role of universities as places of independent, open inquiry is more important than ever.”The two-day event featured lectures by former ICC Judges Raul Cano Pangalangan and Chang-ho Chung on contemporary challenges in international criminal justice, entitled "Duterte before the ICC: Courts as Creatures of Law, or as Creatures of History" and "Jurisprudential Proposals for the Non-State Party Dilemma" respectively, as well as discussions on the APN’s first year, its strategic priorities for 2027, the continued development of national working groups and a roadmap for its medium and long-term sustainability. This Forum forms part of the ICC’s broader Asia-Pacific Engagement Strategy, which seeks to strengthen the Court’s relationships in the region through academic cooperation, capacity building, and outreach. Only 19 States out of the 55 States that make up the Asia-Pacific region are States Parties, making it the region with the lowest representation. This event has shed light on both the importance and viability of deepening cooperation between leading academic institutions, together with the ICC, on matters relating to international criminal law, potentially serving as a model for future engagement in other regions. It has also reflected the shared interest of academia in fostering greater understanding of international criminal justice and encouraging dialogue on related issues. The Court and Keio University are very grateful to the European Union for its generous financial support of this event. The Court also expresses its appreciation for the strong partnership with Keio University in co-hosting this event, as well as to the participating universities, professors, and other contributors for their engagement.For more information, please contact the ICC Public Affairs Unit: PublicAffairs.Unit@icc-cpi.int. You can also follow the Court’s activities on X, Facebook, YouTube, Instagram and Flickr

articles.title: The Lock and the Lever: The Indus Waters Award and the Test of Fundamental Change of Circumstances
articles.description: [Mritunjai Kapila is an incoming Staff Lawyer at Volterra Fietta and holds an Erasmus Mundus LLM in International Law of Global Security, Peace and Development from the University of Glasgow and Le…
paragraphs: [ Mritunjai Kapila is an incoming Staff Lawyer at Volterra Fietta and holds an Erasmus Mundus LLM in International Law of Global Security, Peace and Development from the University of Glasgow and Leuphana University.]

On 31 August 2026, the tribunal constituted under the Indus Waters Treaty 1960 (IWT) unanimously held that the Treaty “has not been suspended or terminated, and remains fully in force” (para 325). Among other grounds, the tribunal rejected India’s reliance on the argument of a change in fundamental circumstances, a result this post does not question. It concerns paragraph 280, which observed that the IWT’s institutional and dispute settlement mechanism allows the parties “to take account of any changed circumstances relevant to their performance under the treaty”. The tribunal was most likely referring to the absorption of new dam technology under the IWT. But the remark is framed generally and sits in the tribunal’s analysis of foreseeability, and raises a question that matters even beyond the IWT: can the existence of treaty machinery show that the parties foresaw a change? This post argues that it can, but only for the kind of change the machinery was designed to accommodate. Read that way, paragraph 280 is sound. However, read as a general rule, it would make the plea of fundamental change of circumstances almost unavailable under any treaty with a commission and a dispute settlement clause, just as climate change and the need for clean energy are prompting arguments for its use.

The IWT divides, rather than shares, the six rivers of the Indus Basin: India receives virtually all of the three Eastern Rivers and, in exchange, must “let flow” the three Western Rivers to Pakistan, subject to a right to operate run-of-river hydropower plants within strict limits (para 283). A Permanent Indus Commission, with one Commissioner from each State, handles cooperation; technical differences may go to a Neutral Expert and disputes to a Court of Arbitration (Article IX).

The case arose from Pakistan’s challenge to the design of India’s Kishenganga and Ratle hydroelectric plants on the Western Rivers. India referred the same questions to a Neutral Expert and did not participate before the tribunal (para 204). From January 2023, India sought to negotiate modifications to the treaty (para 250). On 23 April 2025, the day after the Pahalgam attack killed 26 civilians, India declared that the Treaty would be “held in abeyance with immediate effect” (paras 6, 94).

Under the principle of pacta sunt servanda, “[e]very treaty in force is binding upon the parties to it and must be performed by them in good faith” ( Article 26 of the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties (VCLT), quoted at para 232). The IWT reinforces the principle: it has no withdrawal clause, stays in force “until terminated by a duly ratified treaty concluded for that purpose between the two Governments” (Article XII(4)), and it can be modified only in the same way (Article XII(3)). The tribunal held that Pakistan has no duty to negotiate modifications (para 242) and that a failure to agree, “standing alone, is also not wrongful” (para 252). That is the lock.
articles.lede: On 31 August 2026, the tribunal constituted under the Indus Waters Treaty 1960 (IWT) unanimously held that the Treaty “has not been suspended or terminated, and remains fully in force” (para 325).

articles.title: Georgia: Near-total impunity after two years of human rights violations in response to protests
articles.description: Justice for police violence remains elusive, emboldening further abuses, and the recent release of protesters, and convictions of a handful of police officers for abusive use of force, cannot disguise the scale of continuing injustice.
paragraphs: Ahead of the second anniversary of the start of the ongoing anti-government protests in Georgia, which have been marked by persistent human rights violations and near-total impunity for those responsible, Denis Krivosheev, Amnesty International’s Deputy Director for Eastern Europe and Central Asia, said:

“After two years of escalating government repression, few areas of public and political life remain untouched. From taking steps to outlaw opposition parties and dismantle civil society at large, to the targeting of hundreds for taking part in protest, repression is now deeply woven into the fabric of Georgian society.”

“Artistic expression and political satire are under attack. Musicians have been threatened and fined over protest songs, journalist have been detained over satirical posts, and comedians have been assaulted for making jokes, in an atmosphere or violence spearheaded by the state. What began as a crackdown on street protests has become a daily assault on fundamental rights and freedoms.

“Justice for police violence remains elusive, emboldening further abuses, and the recent release of protesters, and convictions of a handful of police officers for abusive use of force, cannot disguise the scale of continuing injustice, with dozens of people including Mate Devidze still in prison following unfair trials.

“The authorities must investigate allegations of torture and other ill-treatment and bring those suspected of responsibility to justice. They must immediately release everyone imprisoned solely for exercising their human rights and ensure an independent review of all protest-related convictions.”

Justice for police violence remains elusive, emboldening further abuses, and the recent release of protesters, and convictions of a handful of police officers for abusive use of force, cannot disguise the scale of continuing injustice

Since the protests began in November 2024, after disputed parliamentary elections and the freezing of EU accession talks, thousands have faced arbitrary detention and fines, hundreds have reported torture or other ill-treatment, and over 150 individuals were imprisoned after unfair, politically motivated trials.

The intimidation campaign continued to target dissent: musicians Kordzi and Sofo Batilashvili were threatened and fined over protest songs; journalist Vakho Sanaia was twice detained over satirical posts; comedian Onise Okriashvili was assaulted near his home by unknown individuals after a government-encouraged smear campaign. Recently, activist Tornike Razmadze faced threats and smears by pro-state media through AI-generated videos falsely portraying him as a drug dealer.

Over 300 protesters reported torture or other ill-treatment during the November-December 2024 crackdown alone. Only five low-ranking police and special forces officers have been convicted, and no one in command is known to have been charged. In September, activist Sergi Kancheli reported being beaten, threatened at gunpoint and subjected to attempted sexual violence by six police officers. No officers are known to have been charged over these allegations. Allegations of unlawful toxic chemicals used against street protestors also remain without effective investigation.

articles.title: An Abridged Tale of Tuvalu: State Continuity, De-Recognition, and Digital Sovereignty as Responses to Sea-Level Rise
articles.description: On 24 September 2026, the United Nations (‘UN’) General Assembly approved by consensus the first UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise, affirming “the presumption in favour of continued statehood” vis-à…
paragraphs: On 24 September 2026, the United Nations (‘UN’) General Assembly approved by consensus the first UN Declaration on Sea Level Rise, affirming “the presumption in favour of continued statehood” vis-à-vis states threatened with deterritorialization on account of sea-level rise; the most vulnerable being low-lying island states. At COP31 in Antalya this November, Tuvalu’s Prime Minister vowed not to “surrender our future”. But the question of sinking states is not yet closed. A presumption, by its nature, may be rebutted, and the Declaration does not say by whom or on what basis. Upon its formal adoption in October, the United States read the text “not as stating any new legal principle”. The Declaration also does not address the form which a deterritorialized state may assume.

The tale of Tuvalu presses both questions. Its Constitution, amended in 2023, provides that the State shall remain in perpetuity notwithstanding any loss of physical territory; its Future Now Project envisages a ‘digital nation’. There are three running issues here: (1) the continuity of statehood (the external self-determination issue ); (2) the permanence of maritime entitlements (the law of the seas issue ); and (3) the exercise of digital sovereignty (the internal self-determination issue ).

In a longer article forthcoming in the German Law Journal, I focus on the first and third. On the first, I argue that: (1) Tuvalu’s statehood is entirely independent of Montevideo compliance; (2) it continues by virtue of the presumption, which I argue to be a principle since it is temporally unlimited and rebuttable only at the behest of its beneficiary; and (3) states are prohibited from de-recognizing Tuvalu against its will, since de-recognition, rather than the loss of Montevideo criteria, would effectuate its extinction. On the third, I argue that digital sovereignty is a legitimate exercise of a people’s right to choose the internal structure of their state. The arguments apply mutatis mutandis to all threatened low-lying island states.

Taken at face value, the 1933 Montevideo criteria militate against the survival of states submerged by sea-level rise. Scholars have responded by treating the criteria as merely descriptive, as flexibly applied in practice, as satisfied by maritime territory alone, or as a Westphalian conception which invisibilizes indigenous models. A fundamental issue with each of these arguments is the assumption of the automatic relevance of the Montevideo criteria, even if only as a starting point.

I submit that a more convincing argument is as follows: the Montevideo criteria belong to the law of state creation rather than the law of state continuity. As the first category of state existence to possess normative content, state creation unduly lent its normativity to state continuity. Hence, Krystyna Marek’s landmark articulation of the presumption of state continuity held it contingent on the non-permanent disappearance of a state’s ‘material elements’. This position is untenable. First, the restriction to temporary loss only manifests in hindsight: Somalia was treated as continuing regardless of the prospects of restoring its government. Second, as Yejoon Rim explains, state creation and state continuity are fundamentally different processes; once created, a state is a legal fact, over and above the social facts required for its creation. Third, and most importantly, a growing consensus either restricts the Montevideo criteria to state creation or applies the presumption to states facing permanent submersion or land inhabitability. By my count (detailed here ), approximately 135 states support either or both positions, across the Pacific Islands Forum, the Alliance of Small Island States (‘AOSIS’), the Sixth Committee, and the International Court of Justice (‘ICJ’) proceedings in Climate Change (calculated before the count from the UN Declaration). With the unanimous support of specially-affected states, a credible argument could be made that a customary rule is forming.

articles.title: Common Interests and Compensation: What Next?
articles.description: [Dr Niko Pavlopoulos is a Lecturer in Law at UCL Faculty of Laws, University College London.] Introduction In its hotly-waited merits Judgment in The Gambia v Myanmar, the International Court of Ju…
paragraphs: [ Dr Niko Pavlopoulos is a Lecturer in Law at UCL Faculty of Laws, University College London.]

In its hotly-waited merits Judgment in The Gambia v Myanmar, the International Court of Justice held Myanmar responsible for committing genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State, for failing to prevent genocide, for failing to punish genocide, for failing to enact the necessary legislation to give effect to the provisions of the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide (‘Genocide Convention’), and for violating the Court’s 2020 Order on provisional measures (para 646 (1), (2), (4), (5), (12)).

The Court held, moreover, that Myanmar is obliged to adopt certain measures of restitution and, insofar as not made good by restitution, to compensate the Rohingya group and its members for the damage caused by the violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention (paras 646 (9), 646 (10)). The Court has given Myanmar two years to transmit to the Court ‘a report setting out the measures of restitution that it has adopted and, to the extent that full reparation by restitution is materially impossible, specifying the amount and modalities of compensation’ (para 625).

What does this all mean for reparation in erga omnes (partes) cases? This question is the focus of the present post, which notes first the importance of the Court recognizing the entitlement of a non-injured states to request performance of the obligation of reparation (alongside assurances and guarantees of non-repetition) in such cases. The post then turns to unresolved questions concerning the role of a non-injured state, in this case The Gambia, to negotiate, litigate, and supervise the disbursement of any compensation. It outlines a few of the possibilities, suggesting that the Court may in the next couple of years have to consider more seriously whether—and, if so, when—a non-injured state may litigate and supervise the disbursement of compensation in the interest of the beneficiaries of an erga omnes (partes) obligation.

In its 2001 Articles on the Responsibility of States for Internationally Wrongful Acts (ARSIWA), the International Law Commission (ILC) indicated that a non-injured state may invoke the responsibility of another state in respect of an alleged breach of an erga omnes or erga omnes partes obligation. It stipulated, moreover, that, in so doing, a non-injured state may claim from the responsible State cessation of the internationally wrongful act, assurances and guarantees of non-repetition, and performance of the obligation of reparation in the interest of the injured state or of the beneficiaries of the obligation breached (art 48(2)).

At the time the ILC adopted the ARSIWA, it acknowledged that permitting a non-injured state to seek reparation in the interest of the injured state or of the beneficiaries of the obligations breached involved ‘a measure of progressive development, which is justified since it provides a means of protecting the community or collective interest at stake’ (art 48, comment 12).

articles.title: 16 Days of Activism: UNHCR warns over deep funding cuts to vital protection work
articles.description: Serious funding cuts are severely weakening protection for refugee and stateless women and girls and others at risk of gender-based violence (GBV), like Mariam, who survived a decade of captivity and rape at the hands of Boko Haram militia.
paragraphs: “ They come and pick girls ,” Ms. Wosornu, UNHCR Assistant High Commissioner for Protection, told journalists in Geneva on Friday, repeating what Mariam had told her in Nigeria. After escaping her ordeal which had involved attacks by multiple men, she “felt like she was taken out of a fire”, the UNHCR official added.
Last year, 171 UNHCR-supported “safe spaces” for women and girls were forced to close and today, 203 remain open.
When safe spaces shut, specialist services for survivors of attacks and abuse are cut and medical and legal referral options narrow, Ms. Wosornu explained.

The closures are part of a recent erosion of GBV services which left the agency’s programmes to counter the issue less than one-third funded in 2025. In all, 5.6 million forcibly displaced and stateless people have been left without lifesaving prevention and response services, according to UNHCR’s 2025 GBV Impact Report.
The development comes alongside this year’s 16 Days of Activism against Gender-Based Violence campaign, ending 10 December.

“Gender-based violence is one of the most pervasive human rights violations, hence the need for 16 Days (of Activism) and 16 days is certainly not enough,” Ms. Wosornu insisted. “Nearly one in three women globally has experienced some physical and sexual violence. More than 60 million forcibly displaced and stateless women and girls face heightened risks. So, these funding cuts are slashing the very services that are needed to support them. We must not mistake silence for safety.”

She recalled working in Goma, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where survivors recounted their harrowing stories and asking them what they wanted most. “They said, ‘For our perpetrators to face justice.’ And yet, access to justice is one of the serious challenges that we face. Only nine per cent of survivors referred to legal services, due to documentation and language barriers.”

It is often very difficult for many young women survivors to recover from their ordeals, especially since they can face rejection and stigma in their own families and communities. Today, though, Mariam and other survivors receive support and vocational training through a government-run initiative supported by UNHCR and partners.
Despite severe underfunding, the agency’s specialized GBV programmes reached 2.2 million people in 77 countries worldwide in 2025 and the first half of 2026.

articles.title: Ecuador: Justicia para comunidades que defienden el territorio
articles.description: París, Ginebra, 27 de noviembre de 2026. La Federación Internacional por los Derechos Humanos (FIDH) y la Organización Mundial Contra la Tortura (…)
paragraphs: París, Ginebra, 27 de noviembre de 2026. La Federación Internacional por los Derechos Humanos (FIDH) y la Organización Mundial Contra la Tortura (OMCT), en el marco del Observatorio para la Protección de las Personas Defensoras de Derechos Humanos, manifestamos nuestra solidaridad con las comunidades que en Ecuador defienden el territorio, el agua y la naturaleza, y que buscan justicia ante tribunales independientes e imparciales.

El caso de Las Naves (Bolívar): El 4 de noviembre de 2026, un juez de primera instancia declaró improcedente la Acción Constitucional de Protección presentada por las comunidades campesinas del cantón Las Naves, representadas por la CEDHU (organización miembro en Ecuador de la FIDH), contra el Ministerio de Ambiente y Energía y la empresa minera Curimining S.A. por el proyecto Curipamba – El Domo.

Las comunidades desde hace más de 10 años denuncian la vulneración de los derechos de la naturaleza, a un ambiente sano, al agua, a la identidad cultural, al territorio campesino, a la participación y a la consulta ambiental, así como la criminalización de sus líderes y daños a vías, viviendas y fuentes de agua. La decisión será revisada por la Corte Provincial de Justicia de Pichincha. El Observatorio observó el proceso y continuará apoyando su búsqueda de justicia.

El caso de Los Ángeles (Durán, Guayas): El próximo 27 de noviembre, las comunidades campesinas de Los Ángeles, junto con la organización Tierra y Vida, comparecerán ante la Corte Provincial de Justicia de Guayas en la audiencia pública de apelación de su Acción Constitucional de Protección, declarada improcedente en primera instancia, contra el desalojo de 31 familias ordenado en abril de 2025 a petición de la empresa camaronera TRUPECA S.A.S. En este caso, la FIDH presentó un amicus curiae que reclama el reconocimiento de estas familias como defensoras de derechos humanos y subraya que el desalojo está estrechamente ligado a la vulneración de su derecho a defender la tierra.

El extractivismo es hoy uno de los principales focos de conflictividad y de afectación de derechos humanos en Ecuador, como denunció el informe publicado en septiembre de este año: Ataques y criminalización contra la sociedad civil en un contexto de militarización y extractivismo en Ecuador.

La Constitución ecuatoriana fue, y sigue siendo, la única del mundo con un capítulo completo de derechos de la naturaleza. Eso demuestra la importancia de estos derechos: protegerlos no es una facultad discrecional de las autoridades, es una obligación, igual que proteger a las personas y comunidades que los defienden.

Sin embargo, los sectores extractivos (minería, petróleo, agroindustria, pesca y hidroeléctricas) se expanden apoyados en un entramado de decisiones normativas, institucionales y de seguridad que se justifican en el nombre del crecimiento económico y la "seguridad" de las inversiones. Los territorios se convierten así en espacios de disputa, donde los derechos de la naturaleza, los derechos colectivos y las formas de vida de pueblos indígenas, afrodescendientes y comunidades campesinas quedan especialmente expuestos al despojo. Dos ejemplos recientes lo ilustran: – La sustitución de la licencia ambiental integral por una simple autorización administrativa para ciertas actividades mineras (art. 3.a de la Ley Orgánica para el Fortalecimiento de los Sectores Estratégicos); – La norma incluida en la Ley de Transparencia Social y su Reglamento que equipara la oposición a proyectos extractivos con amenazas al orden público y establece sanciones de cierre de las organizaciones por 4 años.

articles.title: How two brothers who disagree with JEP trimmed its budget
articles.description: Together, the Gómez Martínez brothers are at the centre of a campaign led by Abelardo de la Espriella’s new government against Colombia’s transitional justice system: they have succeeded in cutting the budget of the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) – with which they disagree – by a fifth.
paragraphs: Two months ago, Senator Enrique Gómez Martínez proposed a bill with the aim of bringing forward, by five years, the closure date of the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) – the judicial arm of the transitional justice system established under the peace agreement in Colombia. At the same time, Finance Minister Miguel Gómez Martínez spearheaded the approval of Colombia’s national budget, which ended up cutting the JEP’s 2027 funding by about 170 billion pesos (48 million dollars, or a fifth of its current budget), after a legislative process in which one of the proposals supporting the reduction was put forward by his brother.

The actions of both have been consistent with the stance and narrative of their political leader, Abelardo de la Espriella, who promised during his campaign to put an end to a transitional justice system that he previously defended in a self-published book. But the Gómez brothers have also their own history with the JEP: six years ago, the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) claimed responsibility for the murder of their uncle Álvaro Gómez Hurtado, a three-time presidential candidate and one of Colombia’s most prominent politicians of the last half-century.
Although they come from a well-known conservative political dynasty that produced a president and two senators, the Gómez brothers owe their current political success to Abelardo de la Espriella.

Enrique, who had devoted himself to practising law and running the family foundation in honour of his murdered uncle, stood as a presidential candidate in 2022, but won only 0.23 per cent of the vote. His political party, National Salvation – revived thanks to a provision in the peace agreement designed to compensate political groups decimated by the war – only garnered 29,000 votes for the Senate and fell well short of the minimum threshold required to enter Congress.

This year, through an alliance that gave National Salvation a national figurehead and De la Espriella a political party with legal status, they secured four seats in the Senate and one in the House of Representatives. Gómez Martínez has become chair of the Senate’s Constitutional Committee after securing 139,000 votes, the sixth-highest national vote tally.

And once in power, De la Espriella indulged them: he appointed Nicolás Gómez Arenas, Enrique’s son, as his private secretary and chose Miguel as Finance Minister. A former member of Congress, ambassador and Deputy Comptroller, Miguel had been out of the public eye for a decade.
At the end of September, Enrique Gómez introduced a bill proposing that the JEP – which he often refers to as a “farce” – should close its doors after 10 years of operation in March 2028.

The senator’s intention was for the special tribunal to conclude its work on the date its legal deadline for filing indictment expires, despite the fact that its constitutional mandate includes a further five years – that is until 2033 – to complete the handing down of sentences for those charges. This period is crucial for the special tribunal, which has charged 520 people as those most responsible for atrocious crimes committed during the armed conflict but has only convicted 25 so far.

articles.title: « Vous en avez assez tué »: le pasteur Charles Talingano interpelle les mercenaires russes du groupe Wagner
articles.description: Face aux violences des mercenaires russes en Centrafrique, le pasteur Charles Talingano exige la fin des crimes et la reconquête de la dignité.
paragraphs: Le pasteur Charles Talingano fustige les crimes perpétrés par les mercenaires russes du groupe Wagner et exige la libération du peuple centrafricain.

« Wagner n’a qu’à aller faire la liberté de la Russie, mais nous reprenons nos droits. Vous en avez assez tué! » Le pasteur Charles Talingano lance cette mise en demeure directe aux mercenaires russes du groupe Wagner déployés en République centrafricaine. Dans une déclaration d’une rare virulence, l’homme d’Église condamne les tueries commises contre les populations et rejette toute tutelle étrangère qui piétine la dignité des Centrafricains.

Le religieux ne prend aucun gant avec les combattants russes. Il leur reproche ouvertement les morts, les humiliations et le calvaire infligés aux civils sur le territoire national. Pour lui, aucune coopération militaire étrangère ne saurait justifier que des citoyens soient spoliés de leurs droits fondamentaux dans leur propre patrie.
Son intervention prend un tour particulièrement incisif lorsqu’il énumère les exactions commises par ces mercenaires.
« Ne pas laisser les mercenaires venir te dépouiller, te violer, t’introduire à l’humiliation », lance-t-il aux Centrafricains.

Ces accusations sont sans appel. Elles expriment la condamnation ferme par Charles Talingano de méthodes barbares, à l’opposé de toute mission de sécurisation des populations. Sans s’attarder sur des dates ou des localités précises dans cette prise de parole, le pasteur cible directement le sort réservé aux civils et le refus catégorique de toute terreur exercée contre les personnes.
Mais le cœur de sa charge porte sur la reconquête de la liberté. Charles Talingano refuse que les mercenaires russes s’érigent en maîtres absolus des droits des Centrafricains.

Il trace une frontière nette entre les intérêts géopolitiques de la Russie et ceux de la République centrafricaine. Les supplétifs étrangers, martèle-t-il, n’ont aucune légitimité pour dicter aux citoyens l’étendue de leurs libertés.
« Nous ne voyons pas avec les yeux de Wagner, les yeux des mercenaires, les yeux de la mort », déclare-t-il.

Cette formule cinglante résume son rejet de l’emprise militaire russe. Le pasteur oppose la dignité humaine au règne de la peur et du sang. Il rappelle que les Centrafricains possèdent leur propre histoire, leur propre armée et un droit inaliénable à la souveraineté.
articles.lede: Face aux violences des mercenaires russes en Centrafrique, le pasteur Charles Talingano exige la fin des crimes et la reconquête de la dignité.

articles.title: Governing Under Siege: A Guide to the 25th Session of the Assembly of States Parties to the Rome Statute
cats: Bureau of the Assembly of States Parties
articles.description: [Ezequiel Jimenez Martinez is an Adjunct Professor at the Pompeu Fabra Law Faculty, and a Senior Fellow at the Center for International Law Research and Policy. He is the author of Governing the In…
paragraphs: [ Ezequiel Jimenez Martinez is an Adjunct Professor at the Pompeu Fabra Law Faculty, and a Senior Fellow at the Center for International Law Research and Policy. He is the author of Governing the International Criminal Court: the History and Practice of the Assembly of States Parties to the Rome Statute (Brill, 2025).]

On November 30 th the Assembly of States Parties opens its 25th session in The Hague, rather than at United Nations Headquarters, compressed from 11 days into 8. The Bureau moved it because elected officials of the Court, including its President, are under sanctions by the United States, some delegations face visa restrictions and many civil society organizations cannot enter the country, all while insisting that the decision sets no precedent. In 2024 I described the stakes of the 23rd session as high, in 2025 I argued that it was time to act to provide the Court with proper governance. Since then the United States has sanctioned the Court itself, the Assembly has removed the Prosecutor with a questionable procedure, and seven States have deposited notifications of withdrawal while the main reaction has been of quiet regret instead of action. In fact, the only action reported has been an Ambassadorial retreat on how to respond, including accommodation, to the United States’ demands, including possible amendments to the Statute, all in preparation of the 25 th session.

In this context, this session is no longer about how to protect the Court from penalizing sanctions of non-States Parties, but whether the (still) 125 member States care if at all about what the Court stands for, beyond its current challenges. This session will determine what governing the institution looks like at maximum pressure. Will the Assembly agree to break the siege or succumb to external pressures? This post tries to summarize the key issues and decisions coming up as a sort of guide of what to look for when answering the previous question – from responding to sanctions, to electing a new Assembly President and six new judges, to preparing the election of the 4 th Prosecutor, the 2027 budget and overall membership. This Assembly session has the potential to be the fork in the road of accountability for international crimes in the institutional shape of the International Criminal Court.

First, sanctions. On October 9 th the United States designated the Court as an entity under Executive Order 14203. General Licence 13, which allows dealings with the Court to be maintained or wound down, expires on 7 April 2027, and the State Department has presented that window as time for States Parties to make progress on resolutions addressing the United States’ concerns. These concerns are, simply, a deep misunderstandings of how the Rome Statute works and are aligned to a myopic view of the Court by the United States ever since it ‘unsigned’ the Rome Statute. The sanctions now cover 9 of the 18 judges, the President among them, both Deputy Prosecutors, and the former Prosecutor.
articles.lede: On November 30 th the Assembly of States Parties opens its 25th session in The Hague, rather than at United Nations Headquarters, compressed from 11 days into 8.

articles.title: Spain stands alongside victims of international crimes through a voluntary contribution to the Trust Fund for Victims
articles.description: The Kingdom of Spain, a State Party to the International Criminal Court (ICC) since 2000, has made a voluntary contribution totalling EUR 300,000 to the Trust Fund for Victims (TFV), reaffirming its commitment to international justice and the rights of victims of crimes under the Rome Statute. Spain's voluntary contribution is of an unrestricted nature which will support efforts to redress the harm suffered by victims of Rome Statute crimes through the implementation of reparations awards ordered by the ICC, as well as other programmes aimed at their rehabilitation and well-being.This contribution adds to Spain’s continued support to the Trust Fund for Victims, which has progressively contributed towards the full completion of the Court’s first former child soldiers reparations programmes in the Lubanga and Ntaganda cases, and the future programmes for the benefit of victims in situations under the ICC jurisdiction, with an emphasis on Ukraine and Darfur.H.E. Kevin Kelly, Member of the Board of Directors of the TFV stated, “Spain has been a dedicated supporter of the International Criminal Court and the Trust Fund for Victims, demonstrating unwavering assistance to international justice. Its firm support for our mandate reinforces the importance of reparative justice for victims. State contributions are absolutely essential in driving the work of the TFV, especially during these turbulent times, and I implore States to enhance their support for reparative justice in this manner.”H.E. Ms Cecilia Robles Cartes, Ambassador of the Kingdom of Spain to the Kingdom of The Netherlands stated, “The role of the Trust Fund and the International Criminal Court is of vital importance in safeguarding international criminal justice and combating impunity. At a time when the States Parties must strengthen their support for victims, Spain reaffirms its commitment to the Court and to the Rome Statute in the pursuit of peace and justice. Spain also reaffirms its support for the Trust Fund for Victims, helping to ensure reparations and assistance for those who have suffered the consequences of the most serious crimes.”For more information about the Trust Fund for Victims at the ICC, please contact trustfundforvictims@icc-cpi.int or visit www.trustfundforvictims.org. You can also follow TFV’s activities on X, LinkedIn, Bluesky, and Facebook.Background information about the Trust Fund for VictimsVoluntary contributions to the TFV enable the delivery of the reparative mandate of the ICC by funding services and activities that provide recognition, commemoration and material support through rehabilitative programmes. The TFV appeals to States Parties and other entities to contribute to the delivery of reparations to victims in urgent need, particularly in relation to the Ntaganda and Ongwen cases. The annual programme funding target of the TFV is set at a minimum of EUR 10 million. Contributions to the TFV qualify as Official Development Assistance (ODA)-eligible. TFV programmes for the benefit of victims of crimes under the jurisdiction of the ICC contribute to the broader impact of several United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), including peace, justice, and strong institutions (SDG 16), poverty reduction (SDG 1), good health and well-being (SDG 3), gender equality (SDG 5), decent work and economic growth (SDG 8), reduced inequalities (SDG 10), and climate action (SDG 13). For more information about the TFV, please contact trustfundforvictims@icc-cpi.int or visit www.trustfundforvictims.org. You can also follow TFV’s activities on X, LinkedIn, Bluesky, and Facebook.

articles.title: Prison de Ngaragba à Bangui: dénonciations entre détenus, placements au cachot et affrontement entre le régisseur et le chef de sécurité
articles.description: Des tensions éclatent à la prison Ngaragba de Bangui avec un affrontement entre le régisseur et le chef de sécurité sur fond d'isolement au cachot.
paragraphs: La prison centrale de Ngaragba, dans le 7ᵉ arrondissement de Bangui, connaît de fortes tensions entre détenus et responsables pénitentiaires.

Selon l’enquête du CNC, des dénonciations entre prisonniers, des sanctions disciplinaires contestées et des désaccords entre le régisseur et le chef de sécurité alimentent un climat de méfiance au sein de l’établissement.
L’affaire d’un détenu maintenu à plusieurs reprises au cachot, dans des conditions particulièrement difficiles, cristallise aujourd’hui les tensions.
Selon les informations recueillies par la rédaction du CNC, les difficultés trouvent notamment leur origine dans un système de renseignement informel qui fonctionnerait au sein de la prison.
Un détenu, dont l’identité n’est pas encore établie par la rédaction, serait utilisé comme informateur par le régisseur de l’établissement.
Son rôle consisterait à observer les comportements des autres prisonniers, à écouter leurs conversations et à transmettre discrètement au régisseur des informations concernant leurs activités.
C’est ensuite qu’une affaire de vente présumée de tramadol a provoqué une nouvelle série de tensions.

L’informateur aurait signalé au régisseur qu’un prisonnier se livrait à la commercialisation de ce médicament, utilisé illicitement par certaines personnes comme substance psychoactive. À la suite de cette dénonciation, le régisseur serait intervenu directement contre le détenu désigné.
Pourtant, selon les informations recueillies dans le cadre de l’enquête du CNC, le prisonnier mis en cause ne serait pas impliqué dans cette activité de vente de tramadol.

Des éléments recueillis par la rédaction laissent plutôt penser que la dénonciation pourrait être liée à un différend personnel entre les deux détenus. L’hypothèse d’une vengeance est notamment évoquée, même si les circonstances exactes de cette dénonciation restent à établir.
articles.lede: Des tensions éclatent à la prison Ngaragba de Bangui avec un affrontement entre le régisseur et le chef de sécurité sur fond d'isolement au cachot.

My patria is the book: Ten good reads 2026
articles.description: Here, yet again, is my pick of “good reads” from the books I read in 2026. I want to remind you, as I do every year, that these are not “book reviews”, which also explains the relative paucity of l…
paragraphs: Here, yet again, is my pick of “good reads” from the books I read in 2026. I want to remind you, as I do every year, that these are not “book reviews”, which also explains the relative paucity of law books or books about the law. Many excellent ones have come my way this year, as in previous years, but an excellent law book is not always, in fact rarely is, a “good read” in the sense intended here: curl up on the sofa and enjoy a very good read, maybe even as a respite from an excellent law book. I usually point out that some of these “good reads” are not necessarily literary masterpieces—though in the list this year, as is the case every year, each recommendation is for a book which in my eyes is a lot more than a “mere” good read, a handful are truly masterpieces. I dedicate my weekends to reading (hence my preference for slim novels and novellas which can be finished over the weekend. Thus, a lot more than ten good reads came my way this year, don’t they always? I could easily have added another ten. I cheated a bit in the list, offering here and there two or three for the price of one. I trust I will be forgiven.

Some years ago, I warmly recommended Patti Smith’s M Train, as well as mentioning her earlier gem, Just Kids, which described principally her life and times with the controversial photographer Robert Mapplethorpe; M Train was her subsequent rise to fame. What was striking and engaging in both memoirs was not just her huge talent as a writer, but also the richness and depth of her personality and humanity as a young adult.

All that is again in evidence in this new book in which the mature Patti Smith (being seventy-five myself I eschew the word “old”….) offers the story of her life. Even if you are not a fan of Smith the singer and poet—depending on your age you might not even have heard of her—I am sure you will find the book a very good read; it is not just the story of Patti Smith, it is a story of an America that is not often told, a story of the struggles that artists have in a hugely competitive world, all the more difficult for someone like Smith who, admirably, was not willing to compromise her values, and allow the studios and impresarios to take over the management of her persona for commercial reasons. Grant me that this is rare. Socially, this is not a tale of the “high life” of the entertainment world, but of normality where one does not expect it.

What is particularly engaging, even enchanting, is her modesty, even humility (words which typically do not exist in the world of show business), and a wonderfully rare story of a successful, if tragic, marriage. (Yes, occasionally these do exist). And then, Smith has a style all her own—it seems matter of fact, even pedestrian. Its simplicity is its power. I want to believe, as mentioned above, that even those unlike me who do not belong to the Patti Smith “fan club” will find the book satisfying and will not regret curling up on the sofa, losing themselves in a good read.

This novel (her second), by the acclaimed Catalan poetess Eva Baltasar, is of a very different genre. On its face, the story is almost banal. An improbable affair between two women, the “Southern” ship cook, Boulder, and the “Northern” uppity middle-class Samsa, who meet accidently and fall deeply in love. They settle in Reykjavik and share their lives. Samsa moves in the upper echelons of commercial life. Boulder manages a food truck. Yet it works. For all intents and purposes, it is a successful marriage in all but name. But then, predictably (?) and progressively, the relationship frays until their eventual separation. Like a Vivaldi symphony, this is a story told endless times in supposedly different ways, which are all the same. (Apologies to Vivaldi. His Operas are distinct!). So what is different here that makes me recommend this good read with no hesitation?
articles.lede: Here, yet again, is my pick of “good reads” from the books I read in 2026. I want to remind you, as I do every year, that these are not “book reviews”, which also explains the relative paucity of law books or books about the law.

articles.title: A Big Win at The Hague…and the Potential for a Big Win Against Israel
Centrafrique: Libération de l’ancien directeur général du Trésor, Mahamat Abakar, détenu spécial du ministre de la Justice Arnaud Djoubaye Abazène
articles.description: Libéré après vingt mois de détention à Bangui, l'ancien directeur général du Trésor Mahamat Abakar retrouve enfin la liberté en Centrafrique.
paragraphs: L’ancien directeur général du Trésor public, Mahamat Abakar, a été libéré ce mercredi 25 novembre 2026, après plus d’un an et huit mois de détention. Son arrestation, le 11 mars 2025, avait été liée à l’affaire de l’ancien ministre Armel Sayo et à des soupçons de tentative de déstabilisation des institutions centrafricaines.

Sa libération intervient après plusieurs mois de blocage d’une décision judiciaire favorable à sa remise en liberté.Le 11 mars 2025: une arrestation au bureau du ministère des FinancesL’affaire commence le mardi 11 mars 2025. Ce jour-là, des policiers de l’Office central pour la répression du banditisme (OCRB) interpellent Mahamat Abakar directement dans son bureau, au ministère des Finances et du Budget, à Bangui. Il travaillait alors comme coordonnateur du projet AGIR, financé par la Banque mondiale.Ancien directeur général du Trésor public et inspecteur principal du Trésor, il est immédiatement conduit dans les locaux de l’OCRB.

Aucune explication publique précise ne lui est alors fournie sur les motifs de son arrestation.Son interpellation intervient dans le cadre de l’affaire de l’ancien ministre Armel Sayo, arrêté le 17 janvier 2025 à l’aéroport de Douala, au Cameroun. Les enquêteurs cherchent alors à établir d’éventuelles connexions entre plusieurs cadres centrafricains et l’ancien ministre, soupçonné de préparer une déstabilisation du pouvoir de Bangui .Mahamat Abakar est ainsi associé à une supposée entreprise de coup d’État et d’insurrection.
À lire aussi: Ils ont été braqués à 30 km de Boromata: les mercenaires russes et leurs supplétifs sèment le chaos et la panique dans la Vakaga

Lui-même conteste les accusations pendant ses interrogatoires. Lors d’une confrontation avec Boris Toïma, présenté par les enquêteurs comme celui qui aurait cité son nom, ce dernier dément catégoriquement l’avoir dénoncé. Il explique que les policiers lui avaient simplement remis une liste de noms à lire.Son épouse également arrêtée à l’OCRBLe lendemain de son arrestation, l’affaire prend une autre dimension. Son épouse, Zara Salé Djidalbaye, colonel de la douane centrafricaine, se rend à l’OCRB pour lui rendre visite, accompagnée de leur fils.Elle est arrêtée sur place et maintenue en détention jusqu’au 13 mars 2025.
À lire aussi: La mainmise russe: Wagner, Africa Corps et l’étau financier qui va sans doute étouffer la Centrafrique

Leur fils subit également des mauvais traitements policiers avant d’être relâché.Cette arrestation familiale ajoute un nouvel épisode à une affaire qui prend progressivement des proportions considérables.Le ministre de la Justice bloque sa libérationLe plus incompréhensible dans cette affaire intervient en avril 2025. Après examen du dossier, le juge d’instruction Alain Tolmo estime que les éléments disponibles ne justifient pas le maintien en détention de sept personnes, dont Mahamat Abakar.Le magistrat envisage leur libération autour du 11 avril 2025.

Le ministre de la Justice, Arnaud Djoubaye Abazène, intervient alors auprès du juge et s’oppose à cette décision. Selon les informations publiées à l’époque par le CNC, il demande que les suspects soient placés sous mandat de dépôt dans l’attente de son retour du Cameroun.Le 14 avril 2025, les personnes concernées sont finalement envoyées en prison.Mahamat Abakar passe ainsi de la détention à l’OCRB à l’incarcération à la prison de Kondoro. Son maintien en détention se prolonge pendant plusieurs mois, malgré les contestations de son entourage et les démarches entreprises pour obtenir sa libération.Au fil des mois, le CNC publie plusieurs enquêtes sur son dossier, notamment sur les conditions de sa détention, son état de santé et les interventions attribuées au ministre de la Justice.Une libération après plus de vingt mois de détentionCe mercredi 25 novembre 2026, Mahamat Abakar retrouve finalement la liberté.
articles.lede: Libéré après vingt mois de détention à Bangui, l'ancien directeur général du Trésor Mahamat Abakar retrouve enfin la liberté en Centrafrique.

articles.title: Free Education Is Key to Ending Child Marriage
articles.description: On November 27, the world marks the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage – a chance to end a practice that robs children of their childhood and prospects.
paragraphs: On November 27, the world marks the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage – a chance to end a practice that robs children of their childhood and prospects. Every year, 12 million girls are married before 18 – that’s one every three seconds.

Free education is a powerful tool to help prevent it. UNICEF estimates that if all girls completed secondary education, it could cut child marriage by two-thirds. Yet school fees and indirect costs — uniforms, transport, books, examinations — force girls out of school and into early marriage. Free secondary education helps keep girls in school through adolescence, when the risk of child marriage is greatest. Evidence from 14 African countries shows that making lower secondary education free and compulsory raised girls’ educational attainment by 1.6 years.

And prevention needs to start earlier. A study published this month, covering women across 117 countries, found that legal guarantees of pre-primary education were associated with higher rates of school completion among girls and lower rates of child marriage and adolescent childbearing. Yet UNESCO reports that only 68 percent of countries and 46 percent of low-income countries legally guarantee tuition-free pre-primary education.
Free education from pre-primary through secondary forms a continuous pathway to opportunity and empowerment.

Sierra Leone shows what political leadership can achieve on both fronts. Its First Lady spearheaded this International Day, while its education ministers and diplomats have championed a new treaty on free education at the United Nations. Domestically, it has guaranteed 13 years of free education, from pre-primary through secondary, since 2023 and banned child marriage in 2024.

International law needs to catch up. The Convention on the Rights of the Child neither explicitly recognizes a right to early childhood care and education nor guarantees free pre-primary and secondary education for all. Sierra Leone, the Dominican Republic, Bulgaria and ten other countries are therefore advancing a new Optional Protocol to close these gaps. A binding commitment would strengthen accountability and drive national reforms. Negotiations on this proposed treaty will continue in October 2027.

On this inaugural International Day, Sierra Leone, supported by 14 countries, will bring diplomats, experts, and child advocates together in Geneva. Investing in free education advances girls’ rights, dignity, and futures – and is a decisive step towards ending child marriage. By supporting the Optional Protocol at the United Nations, states will be making a clear statement that they stand against child marriage and are committed to delivering a freer and fairer world for girls.
articles.lede: On November 27, the world marks the first International Day for the Elimination of Child, Early and Forced Marriage – a chance to end a practice that robs children of their childhood and prospects.

articles.title: Centrafrique: sept ans après le lancement du DDR, des centaines d’ex-combattants attendent toujours leur intégration dans les forces nationales
articles.description: Des centaines d’ex-combattants en Centrafrique demeurent sans intégration dans les forces nationales, malgré des promesses de réinsertion. Que va faire le
paragraphs: Centrafrique: sept ans après le lancement du DDR, des centaines d’ex-combattants attendent toujours leur intégration dans les forces nationales

Depuis plusieurs années, le gouvernement centrafricain et la MINUSCA annoncent la poursuite du désarmement, de la démobilisation et de la réinsertion des combattants des groupes armés. Sur le terrain, certains ex-combattants attendent encore l’application des engagements pris après leur désarmement.

Le processus de désarmement, démobilisation, réintégration et rapatriement constitue l’un des principaux volets de la politique de paix en République centrafricaine. Il s’inscrit notamment dans le cadre de l’Accord politique pour la paix et la réconciliation (APPR-RCA), signé le 6 février 2019. ￼
À lire aussi: Merci la MINUSCA: « Mission accomplie », peuple trahi, dictature sanglante instaurée 40 ans après Bokassa
Depuis, les annonces sur le DDR se succèdent. Le gouvernement et la MINUSCA présentent régulièrement les opérations de désarmement comme une étape importante vers le retour à la paix.
À lire aussi: Agression d’un conducteur à Carnot par un policier: la décision spectaculaire et étonnante du commissaire adjoint

Le désarmement constitue une première étape. Il doit normalement être suivi d’une démobilisation, puis d’une réintégration dans la vie civile ou, pour certains éléments répondant aux critères prévus, d’une intégration au sein des forces de défense et de sécurité.

La MINUSCA indique qu’après leur désarmement et leur démobilisation, les ex-combattants reçoivent une carte attestant leur nouveau statut et peuvent ensuite accéder aux dispositifs de réintégration. ￼
Le 19 avril 2025, un nouvel accord conclu à N’Djamena a relancé le processus concernant notamment l’Union pour la paix en Centrafrique ( UPC) et le groupe Retour, Réclamation et Réhabilitation (3R).
La dynamique a ensuite été formellement relancée à Bangui en juillet 2025. Les opérations de DDR concernant ces deux groupes ont commencé le 11 juillet 2025 dans plusieurs préfectures. ￼
articles.lede: Centrafrique: sept ans après le lancement du DDR, des centaines d’ex-combattants attendent toujours leur intégration dans les forces nationales

articles.title: Centrafrique: le Réseau des défenseurs des droits de l’homme en Centrafrique accuse certains éléments des forces de défense et de sécurité de violations des droits humains
articles.description: Le REDAC accuse les forces de sécurité de violations des droits de l'homme en Centrafrique à travers des barrières illégales et des abus.
paragraphs: Le Réseau des défenseurs des droits de l’homme en Centrafrique ( REDAC) met en cause certains éléments des forces de défense et de sécurité dans des violations des droits humains rapportées à travers le pays.

Cette position a été exposée par Maître Bruno Yacinth Piegba, vice-président du Réseau des défenseurs des droits de l’homme en Centrafrique, lors d’un entretien consacré à la situation des droits humains en 2026.
Selon lui, des personnes chargées de protéger la population seraient elles-mêmes impliquées dans certains actes portant atteinte aux droits fondamentaux.
« Les droits de l’homme sont violés par certains de ceux qui sont chargés de les protéger », a déclaré Maître Yacinth Piegba.
À lire aussi: Centrafrique: les victimes de la Séléka saluent le verdict contre Mahamat Said et réclament la suite de la justice
À lire aussi: Aboulkassim Algoni, auteur de l’attaque d’Am Dafock, arrêté à N’Djamena: Wagner tente en vain de le faire libérer
Le responsable du REDAC cite notamment la multiplication des barrières illégales comme un exemple concret de violations dénoncées par son organisation.
Il rappelle que les autorités ont adopté un texte interdisant ces barrières. Malgré cette interdiction, certaines continueraient d’exister sur plusieurs axes routiers.
« Les barrières illégales continuent de survivre parce qu’il y a des gens qui continuent de violer ces lois-là », affirme-t-il.

Maître Yacinth Piegba attribue l’installation de certaines de ces barrières à des éléments des forces de défense et de sécurité. Il cite notamment les routes de Damara, Bambari, Bangassou, Mbaïki et Boali.
articles.lede: Le REDAC accuse les forces de sécurité de violations des droits de l'homme en Centrafrique à travers des barrières illégales et des abus.

articles.title: Making the Necessary Possible: A Model Ecocide Law for Latin America
articles.description: [Rodrigo Lledó is an international human rights lawyer and Americas Director at Stop Ecocide International.] Taking Nature Seriously The 20th century left us with the painful lesson that humanity&#…
paragraphs: [ Rodrigo Lledó is an international human rights lawyer and Americas Director at Stop Ecocide International.]

The 20th century left us with the painful lesson that humanity’s greatest horrors were committed when power, blinded by dogmas and ideologies of one kind or another, stripped individuals of their intrinsic dignity. To confront this barbarism, the law had to be reimagined.

During my studies in the philosophy of law at the Universidad Carlos III de Madrid, I had the opportunity to study the best known work of the American jurist Ronald Dworkin, Taking Rights Seriously. Dworkin argued that fundamental rights must act as true “trumps” against State abuses and the arbitrary actions of majorities.

However, the 21st century has brought new dimensions to longstanding injustices. Driven by an insatiable demand for natural resources, environmental destruction is accelerating across the planet, degrading ecosystems and threatening the communities that depend on them. Indigenous peoples, already subjected to centuries of dispossession, exploitation and discrimination, face growing pressures as extractive activities expand into their territories and the environmental foundations of their livelihoods and cultures are eroded. Many of these communities have maintained profound relationships with the natural world across generations, embodying principles of ecological balance and collective wellbeing reflected in the concept of buen vivir (good living).

Faced with this devastation, “serious” measures are needed—of greater depth and efficacy than mere reprimands or administrative fines, which large corporations tend to absorb as a mere operating cost on their balance sheets.
The last century marked a profound advance in justice as we learned to take human rights seriously, today the ethical and legal imperative demands that we take Nature seriously.

This implies a qualitative leap: articulating effective criminal responses capable of punishing the mass destruction of the environment. The Earth is not an inexhaustible source of natural resources; it is a finite place, the shared home of all species, including our own.
As I have pointed out elsewhere, international conventions and frameworks such as the Escazú Agreement have marked valuable milestones, but it is essential to go further.

In 2021, I had the privilege of being part of the International Expert Panel convened by the Stop Ecocide Foundation to draft an international legal definition of ecocide, designed to be incorporated into the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court. We were twelve jurists from five continents, of whom two represented Latin America. That effort crystallised in a precise definition: unlawful or wanton acts committed with knowledge that there is a substantial likelihood of severe and either widespread or long-term damage to the environment.

However, when bringing this international definition into domestic legislation—especially in countries with a Roman-Germanic tradition, known in the English-speaking world as civil law —it requires a process of adaptation. This must, moreover, be done in harmony and consonance with the international definition to maintain coherence and unity of meaning.
articles.lede: The 20th century left us with the painful lesson that humanity’s greatest horrors were committed when power, blinded by dogmas and ideologies of one kind or another, stripped individuals of their intrinsic dignity.

articles.title: In This Issue
articles.description: In the Book Review section of this issue, we invite readers to reflect on the language of international law and on the significance of the concepts, vocabularies and interpretive frameworks through…
paragraphs: In the Book Review section of this issue, we invite readers to reflect on the language of international law and on the significance of the concepts, vocabularies and interpretive frameworks through which it seeks both to apprehend and to constitute the realities over which it claims authority. This invitation extends equally to the meanings that may be attributed to the writings and pronouncements of state representatives and to the legal significance of the silences kept by states themselves.
We begin with two Review Essays on a series of books addressing different dimensions of what has come to be known as the question of Palestine.

The first Review Essay is written by Michelle Burgis-Kasthala. Drawing on the works under review, she raises fundamental questions about how scholars can approach the subject, both substantively and stylistically. Can the conflict still be addressed through the rules and principles of international human rights law and by invoking the role of international institutions entrusted with their implementation? Or does it require a more fundamental rethinking of the structures and dynamics of the international legal order, whose limitations – or even futility – the war in Gaza appear to have laid bare? Should scholars remain committed to the two-state solution, or turn their attention and intellectual imagination to considering what a single-state reality could entail? To what extent do focus on compliance with the law of armed conflict contribute to legitimizing the war and its outcomes, while displacing political debates on a lasting solution for the region? What temporal continuities and ruptures underpin scholarly studies on Palestine? Can one write about the conflict without acknowledging the impact of its traumatic nature on the ways in which analysis may be framed?

The second Review Essay is penned by Michael Karayanni. In his view, all the five works he discusses illustrate the extent to which Palestinians have been denied their rights and subjected to policies that position them as inferior to other groups. They further suggest that such practices of dispossession and subordination have, at times, been facilitated and even entrenched by international law itself. In this respect, Karayanni argues, the books share an ambition akin to that of scholars associated with Third World Approaches to International Law (TWAIL), namely, to develop a language of international law capable of rendering visible the imperial and colonial interests that it continues to serve, as it has done since the nineteenth century. He finally submits that a Third World approach to private international law may likewise illuminate the ways in which courts and tribunals adjudicating private disputes can reinforce the hegemonic interests of the states within which they operate.

We then turn to Ben Chester Cheong’s review of Lys Kulamadayil’s monograph, The Pathology of Plenty: Natural Resources in International Law, a work that may similarly be situated within TWAIL scholarship. The book seeks to explain how principles celebrated as legal victories of decolonization – most notably permanent sovereignty over natural resources – helped create the conditions for contemporary regimes of extraction. In Cheong’s assessment, Kulamadayil persuasively demonstrates that resource sovereignty was designed not to restrain extraction but to enable it, thereby revealing international law not merely as a flawed language, but as one deliberately structured to facilitate the accumulation of capital.
articles.lede: In the Book Review section of this issue, we invite readers to reflect on the language of international law and on the significance of the concepts, vocabularies and interpretive frameworks through which it seeks both…

articles.title: AEP25: les États Parties doivent traduire leur soutien à la justice internationale en actions concrètes
articles.description: 2026/11/26 AEP25: les États Parties doivent traduire leur soutien à la justice internationale en actions concrètes Introductory text: Ce mois-ci, la 25ème session de l’Assemblée des États Parties au Statut de Rome de la CPI se tiendra à La Haye, du 30 novembre au 7 décembre 2026, dans un contexte d’intensification des attaques contre l’indépendance de la Cour pénale internationale, ses activités et les personnes et organisations qui rendent son travail possible. À l’approche de la session, la Coalition pour la Cour pénale internationale (CCPI) publie son document de référence pour l’AEP25. S’a
paragraphs: Les sanctions visant l’institution menacent des services essentiels, les mandats d’arrêt restent inexécutés et les organisations de la société civile subissent des représailles pour leurs efforts en faveur de la lutte contre l’impunité. Pour les victimes et les personnes survivantes, ces attaques menacent la perspective même d’obtenir justice. Alors que les États Parties se préparent à se réunir pour leur session annuelle, ils doivent traduire leurs engagements envers le Statut de Rome en mesures concrètes de protection, en ressources et en coopération.

Dans le même temps, la Cour et les organisations de la société civile poursuivent leur travail avec détermination. Deux procès doivent s’ouvrir dans les situations en Libye et aux Philippines, ouvrant la voie à une justice attendue depuis longtemps par des milliers de victimes.
Lors de l’AEP25, les États Parties doivent démontrer que leur engagement envers le Statut de Rome s’accompagne des décisions, des ressources et des mesures pratiques nécessaires à sa défense.

Cette année a mis en évidence tant les possibilités offertes par la justice internationale que la fragilité des conditions dont elle dépend. Les procédures relatives aux situations aux Philippines et en Libye ont ouvert des perspectives attendues de longue date pour que les voix des victimes soient entendues. La société civile a continué de documenter les crimes, de soutenir les personnes survivantes et d’exiger que les responsables rendent des comptes. Pourtant, ces efforts se déploient dans un contexte de sanctions, d’ingérences politiques, de défauts d’exécution des mandats d’arrêt et de pressions financières qui menacent la capacité de la Cour à rendre justice.

La désignation de la CPI en tant qu’institution visée par des sanctions américaines le 9 octobre 2026 a marqué une escalade majeure des attaques qui ciblaient déjà des responsables de la Cour et des organisations de la société civile. Les conséquences dépassent les personnes et entités directement sanctionnées: les restrictions touchant les services bancaires, technologiques et autres services essentiels perturbent le travail de lutte contre l’impunité, tandis que la menace de nouvelles mesures décourage la coopération et isole les personnes qui cherchent à obtenir justice. Les pressions exercées sur les États Parties pour qu’ils reconsidèrent leur adhésion au Statut de Rome menacent également la portée du système et leur capacité à respecter leurs engagements sans subir de coercition extérieure.

Ces attaques coïncident avec des manquements persistants à l’obligation de coopérer avec la Cour. L’exécution des mandats d’arrêt dépend de l’action des États, mais les considérations politiques continuent d’y faire obstacle. Les renvois à l’Assemblée concernant l’ Italie et le Tadjikistan lui confèrent une responsabilité particulière: veiller à ce que les constats judiciaires de non-coopération fassent l’objet d’un suivi politique et diplomatique soutenu. Pour les victimes et les témoins, l’absence d’arrestation et de remise des personnes suspectes peut prolonger l’insécurité, renforcer les craintes de représailles et ébranler la confiance dans la capacité de leur participation aux travaux de la Cour à contribuer à la lutte contre l’impunité.
