articles.title: Philippines: Duterte trial a defining test for justice, accountability and future of the ICC
articles.description: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte's trial at the ICC for alleged crimes against humanity is a historic opportunity for justice for victims of the so-called "war on drugs".
paragraphs: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte’s trial at the International Criminal Court (ICC) for crimes against humanity is a historic opportunity for justice for victims of the so-called “war on drugs” and a defining test for the future of international accountability, Amnesty International said ahead of the trial starting on Monday 30 November.

The trial, which will focus on murders and attempted murders allegedly committed between 2013 and 2019 while Duterte was President of the Philippines and Mayor of Davao City, opens at a time when the ICC is facing unprecedented attacks from the US government and other powerful states.

“For thousands of families of victims, this trial represents something they have been denied for years: the chance to see those allegedly responsible for horrific crimes brought before a court of law,” said Ritz Lee Santos III, Executive Director of Amnesty International Philippines.

“The victims and survivors of the so-called ‘war on drugs’ have shown extraordinary courage and determination in pursuing justice. They must remain at the centre of these proceedings every step of the way.”

Duterte was arrested by the Philippine authorities in March 2025 and surrendered to the ICC to face charges of murder and attempted murder as crimes against humanity linked to the deadly anti-drugs campaign carried out during his presidency, and while he was mayor of Davao City.

During Duterte’s presidential term from 2016 to 2022, thousands of people, predominantly from poor and marginalized communities, were unlawfully killed by police officers or by armed individuals alleged to have links to the police as part of the government’s supposed “war on drugs”.

Duterte’s trial begins less than two months after the Trump administration intensified its campaign against the ICC. On 9 October 2026, the US government imposed sanctions against the institution as a whole, introducing sweeping financial and technological restrictions that will – without state party protection – significantly undermine the Court’s ability to function. The measures are an extension of an Executive Order signed by President Trump on 6 February 2025 authorizing sanctions against the Court, its staff and those cooperating with it.

“Duterte’s trial is a powerful reminder that no one should be beyond the reach of justice. At a moment when the ICC itself is under increasing attack, these proceedings demonstrate why the world must defend the Court’s independence and ability to hold even the most powerful to account under international law,” said Agnès Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International.

“The EU and G7’s unwillingness to protect the ICC and their appeasement in the face of US sanctions represent a betrayal of the victims of grave human rights violations in the Philippines’ poorest neighbourhoods and others around the world. These powerful, privileged leaders are trampling on people’s rights and their hopes of justice.”

The consequences of US sanctions reach far beyond the Philippines. Victims seeking justice through ICC investigations in Ukraine, Palestine, Venezuela, Sudan’s Darfur region, Afghanistan and elsewhere could all be affected if the Court and those working with it are prevented from carrying out their work.
articles.lede: Former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte's trial at the ICC for alleged crimes against humanity is a historic opportunity for justice for victims of the so-called "war on drugs".

articles.title: Sri Lanka: UN report underscores need to end decades-long impunity for conflict-related crimes
articles.description: Responding to the publication of a new report by the UN Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) on crimes under international law committed during Sri Lanka’s 25-year internal armed conflict, Smriti Singh, Amnesty International’s South Asia Director, said: “This report shines a light on the fact that no progress has been…
paragraphs: “This report shines a light on the fact that no progress has been made in addressing crimes under international law in Sri Lanka and that truth, justice and reparation remain elusive for hundreds and thousands of victims. Its findings reflect the unwillingness of successive Sri Lankan governments to investigate allegations and ensure accountability for abuses committed during the internal armed conflict that ended in 2009. Impunity persists even as mass graves continue to be identified, such as in Chemmani where recent exhumations found the remains of more than 583 individuals, including children.

“At a time when conflicts across the world have seen humanitarian assistance and infrastructure come under rampant attack amid a clear disregard for international law, this report is particularly timely. It is significant that it highlights that attacks on humanitarian activities in Sri Lanka became a model and a precursor to what we are seeing in today’s conflicts. This should act as a powerful reminder of how a lack of accountability and continuing impunity in Sri Lanka can be a source of encouragement for those who commit crimes and undermine international law elsewhere.
This report and the Sri Lankan government’s decades-long failure to address justice, truth and reparation underscore the clear need for continued international scrutiny

“This report and the Sri Lankan government’s decades-long failure to address justice, truth and reparation underscore the clear need for continued international scrutiny. This further reinforces the importance of continuing the valuable work of OHCHR’s Sri Lanka Accountability Project and for UN member states to use the project’s resources to advance accountability including through the principles of universal jurisdiction.”

The report, ’I DIED MANY TIMES” Attacks on humanitarian assistance in Sri Lanka, 20 years on’ is available here. The report addresses attacks on humanitarian personnel and operations, and the restriction and denial of humanitarian assistance by all parties, during the final phase of the armed conflict in Sri Lanka.

The OHCHR Sri Lanka Accountability Project (OSLAP) was established by OHCHR to implement the accountability mandate set out in UN Human Rights Council Resolution 46/1 (2021), which requested the Office to “collect, consolidate, analyse and preserve evidence of serious human rights violations and abuses and related crimes in Sri Lanka”.
articles.lede: “This report shines a light on the fact that no progress has been made in addressing crimes under international law in Sri Lanka and that truth, justice and reparation remain elusive for hundreds and thousands of victims.

articles.title: ‘Come right now’: How a crisis centre in Samarkand helps women escape violence
articles.description: Irina* paced the apartment. Her husband had come home drunk again, and she knew the beatings would follow.
paragraphs: Pregnant, with two young children and no close relatives in Samarkand, she called a familiar number with trembling hands: the Rahmdillik (“Compassion”) crisis centre, where she had sheltered before. “Come right now,” came the reply.
Behind a heavy iron gate of an old mansion in central Samarkand lies a small courtyard, where a huge, spreading persimmon tree hangs laden with ripe fruit.

Women of all ages – some in traditional Uzbek dress and headscarves, others in robes or tracksuits – smile warmly at visitors. Each has her own story, but all have fled violence or been left without shelter or any means of support.

A small UN delegation led by Sabine Mahl, the UN Resident Coordinator in Uzbekistan, is welcomed by the centre’s founder, Bibisora Oripova, who points out the latest improvements: a large new television, another renovated room and a sewing workshop.
Dr. Oripova, a surgeon with many years of experience, opened Rahmdillik in 1996. The idea had come to her earlier, while she was working in the burns unit of a local hospital.
“Our unit had many women and children who had suffered burns, were disfigured and had become disabled. Often, their husbands refused to take them back. Where could they go?

“In the Soviet Union, treatment was free, so they stayed in hospital – practically living there. But eventually that was no longer possible,” she says. “I went to the hokim [local official] and asked for a dormitory or some other building where I could shelter women who had nowhere to live.”
As demand grew, the centre expanded, with support from the government and external donors, including UN agencies. Over the years, hundreds of women have passed through its doors.

“We are a traditional society. Some families still do not want women to study or work; they marry them off young. Women have children and do the housework. They are entirely dependent on their husbands’ families,” Dr. Oripova says.
articles.lede: Irina* paced the apartment. Her husband had come home drunk again, and she knew the beatings would follow.

articles.title: Centrafrique: devenus juges et procureurs, les Wagner noirs imposent leur propre code de procédure pénale à la population et sèment le chaos à Gordil
articles.description: À Gordil, les Wagner noirs imposent un système judiciaire arbitraire avec des tarifs exorbitants et procèdent à des arrestations en Centrafrique.
paragraphs: 25 000 francs CFA pour ouvrir une procédure, 75 000 francs pour abandonner une affaire: à Gordil, les Wagner noirs ont instauré leur propre système judiciaire, avec des tarifs sortis directement de leurs chapeaux et imposés aux plaignants et des arrestations pour ceux qui contestent leurs exigences.
Pour comprendre l’ampleur de cette histoire, il faut aller sur le chantier aurifère de Mandjam, situé à une dizaine de kilomètres du centre de Gordil, dans la préfecture de la Vakaga.

En effet, la semaine dernière, deux ouvriers travaillant sur ce site minier se retrouvent en désaccord autour d’une somme de 25 000 francs CFA. Un différend qui, dans le fonctionnement habituel des communautés, aurait pu être soumis au chef du village pour trouver une solution. Selon la nature du problème, les protagonistes peuvent également solliciter les autorités administratives ou les services de sécurité comme la gendarmerie, la police ou encore les soldats FACA.

Mais à Gordil, la situation est différente. Les Wagner noirs, ces miliciens d’autodéfense formés par le groupe Wagner et qui exercent leur autorité sur la localité, se sont progressivement substitués aux autorités compétentes. Ce sont eux qui décident désormais de recevoir les plaintes et de régler les différends entre habitants et faire le boulot des douaniers, policiers, gendarmes, phytosanitaires et autres.
À lire aussi: Centrafrique: Martial Pabandji dénonce la peur, les menaces et la disparition progressive de la liberté d’expression sous le régime de Faustin-Archange Touadéra

Et ce n’est pas tout! Avant même d’examiner le problème opposant les deux ouvriers, les miliciens leur imposent une première condition financière. Chaque partie doit verser 25 000 francs CFA au titre des frais de table. Autrement dit, pour un différend portant sur 25 000 francs CFA, les deux protagonistes doivent réunir ensemble 50 000 francs CFA avant même que leur affaire soit examinée.
À lire aussi: De la Sorbonne à Bangui: premier coup juridique mondial contre les bourreaux de Wagner, Les victimes centrafricaines ne sont plus oubliées

Face à cette exigence, les intéressés protestent. Ils expliquent ne pas disposer d’une telle somme et rappellent qu’ils sont justement venus solliciter une intervention pour régler leur différend. Ils proposent de verser au maximum 5 000 francs CFA, une somme qu’ils estiment déjà difficile à réunir.

La réponse des Wagner noirs est sans appel. Les miliciens leur expliquent que personne ne les rémunère, que le président Faustin-Archange Touadéra ne leur verse aucun salaire et qu’ils doivent donc trouver eux-mêmes les moyens de se payer. Ils maintiennent ainsi leur exigence de 25 000 francs CFA pour chacune des parties.

Devant l’impossibilité de réunir cet argent, les protagonistes décident finalement de renoncer au règlement de leur différend. Mais même cette décision leur coûte cher. Les Wagner noirs leur réclament alors 75 000 francs CFA pour abandonner l’affaire. Une nouvelle exigence que les intéressés ne comprennent pas, puisqu’ils n’ont déjà pas les moyens de payer les premiers frais imposés.
articles.lede: À Gordil, les Wagner noirs imposent un système judiciaire arbitraire avec des tarifs exorbitants et procèdent à des arrestations en Centrafrique.

articles.title: Tunisie: Chaïma Issa entame une grève de la faim ouverte en purgeant une peine de vingt ans de prison dans l'« affaire du complot »
articles.description: TUN 006 / 1126 / OBS 060 Détention arbitraire / Grève de la faim Tunisie 26 novembre 2026 L’Observatoire pour la protection des défenseur·es (…)
paragraphs: L’Observatoire pour la protection des défenseur·es des droits humains, un partenariat de la Fédération internationale pour les droits humains (FIDH) et de l’Organisation mondiale contre la torture (OMCT), vous prie d’intervenir sur la situation suivante en Tunisie.

L’Observatoire a été informé de la grève de la faim ouverte entamée par Mme Chaïma Issa, journaliste, militante politique et défenseure des droits humains, membre du Front de salut national et cofondatrice du collectif « Citoyens contre le coup d’État ». Détenue depuis le 29 novembre 2025, Chaïma Issa purge actuellement une peine de vingt ans d’emprisonnement prononcée dans l’affaire dite du « complot contre la sûreté de l’État ».

Le 16 novembre 2026, Mme Issa a engagé une grève de la faim pour contester son maintien en détention et une condamnation qu’elle dénonce comme inique, prononcée à l’issue de procès dépourvus des garanties fondamentales d’un procès équitable. Dans un communiqué rendu public le 17 novembre 2026, sa famille a relayé ses mots: « Une vie sans liberté n’est pas une vie; c’est une mort lente ». Son avocate, Me Dalila Ben Mbarek Msaddek, a confirmé l’entrée en grève de la faim de sa cliente.

Le 24 novembre 2026, un membre de sa famille qui lui a rendu visite en prison a fait état d’une détérioration préoccupante de son état de santé. Selon son témoignage, Mme Issa aurait perdu du poids et aurait été transférée à deux reprises à l’hôpital au cours de la semaine. Elle éprouverait désormais de grandes difficultés à se déplacer seule et à s’exprimer, les agents pénitentiaires devant l’aider à marcher. Malgré les appels de sa famille à interrompre sa grève de la faim, Mme Issa demeure déterminée à la poursuivre, ce qu’elle considère comme son dernier moyen de résistance et de faire entendre sa voix.

L’Observatoire rappelle qu’il s’agit de la troisième grève de la faim de Mme Issa depuis son incarcération. Dès le jour de son arrestation, le 29 novembre 2025, elle avait cessé de s’alimenter pour dénoncer les violences subies lors de son interpellation, au cours de laquelle elle a été blessée au pied. Elle avait suspendu ce mouvement le 16 décembre 2025. Le 3 février 2026, elle avait également rejoint la grève de la faim périodique initiée par l’avocat et défenseur des droits humains Me Ayachi Hammami, lui aussi détenu dans la même affaire. Ces grèves successives font peser un risque sérieux sur son intégrité physique.

L’Observatoire rappelle que Mme Issa a été violemment arrêtée le 29 novembre 2025 par des policiers en civil, alors qu’elle participait à une manifestation pacifique à Tunis dénonçant la répression des voix dissidentes, puis incarcérée à la prison civile pour femmes de la Manouba. Son arrestation est intervenue au lendemain de l’arrêt rendu fin novembre 2025 par la Cour d’appel de Tunis dans l’« affaire du complot », qui a porté sa peine de dix-huit à vingt ans d’emprisonnement. Le 18 avril 2025, le tribunal de première instance de Tunis avait condamné 37 personnes dans cette affaire, parmi lesquelles des opposant·es politiques, des avocat·es et des défenseur·es des droits humains. Selon les informations disponibles, la Cour de cassation a confirmé le 3 septembre 2026 les condamnations de 34 accusé·es, épuisant ainsi les voies de recours internes.

articles.title: À l’ONU, Touadéra fait un discours pour l’étranger, une dictature pour les Centrafricains
articles.description: Découvrez comment le régime de Touadéra camoufle derrière ses discours internationaux la dictature et le pillage imposés aux Centrafricains.
paragraphs: Il y a deux Touadéra. Celui qui parle à New York, costume bien repassé, ton grave, vocabulaire choisi, regard tourné vers les caméras du monde entier. Et celui qui règne à Bangui, entouré de mercenaires, de milices et de courtisans, loin des micros, loin des projecteurs, loin de toute reddition de comptes. Le premier prononce des discours que l’on pourrait presque croire sincères. Le second impose une réalité que personne, en Centrafrique, ne peut ignorer. Entre les deux, il y a un abîme. Et cet abîme, c’est le peuple centrafricain qui le paie, chaque jour, dans sa chair, dans sa dignité, dans sa survie.

Devant l’Assemblée générale des Nations unies, Touadéra a prononcé un discours taillé pour l’étranger. Un discours lisse, policé, humaniste, presque émouvant par moments. « Je prends la parole au nom de la République Centrafricaine avec le sentiment de responsabilité que confère cette tribune », a-t-il déclaré, comme s’il était l’incarnation de cette responsabilité. Mais la responsabilité, monsieur le Président, ce n’est pas un sentiment que l’on déclame. C’est un acte que l’on pose. Et les actes de Touadéra, depuis huit ans, sont ceux d’un homme qui a choisi la survie de son clan plutôt que la dignité de son peuple. « La fierté d’un peuple qui n’a jamais cessé d’espérer », a-t-il ajouté. Mais de quel peuple parle-t-il? Pas de celui qui vit sous la menace permanente des mercenaires de Wagner et d’Africa Corps. Pas de celui qui a vu ses villages brûler, ses filles violées, ses fils tués. Pas de celui qui, dans les provinces, ne sait pas si demain un camion de mercenaires viendra piller ce qu’il lui reste.

Le discours pour l’étranger, c’est celui de la paix, de la confiance, de la transformation. « Cette session s’ouvre sur le signe d’une double exigence, restaurer la confiance et gérer la transformation », a-t-il affirmé. Mais la confiance ne se restaure pas avec des mots. Elle se restaure avec des actes. Et les actes de Touadéra sont ceux d’un homme qui a trahi la confiance de son peuple. Il a trahi les électeurs en confisquant les élections de 2020. Il a trahi les opposants en les emprisonnant ou en les exilant. Il a trahi les journalistes en muselant la presse. Il a trahi les victimes en refusant de les écouter. Il a trahi la Centrafrique en la vendant au plus offrant. « Nous n’avons jamais eu autant de raisons d’agir ensemble et jamais autant de mal à le faire », a-t-il lancé, dans un de ces paradoxes dont il a le secret. Mais ce mal à agir ensemble, il l’incarne d’abord à l’échelle de son propre pays, où il a préféré diviser, réprimer et s’allier à des forces étrangères plutôt que de construire un État de droit.

La dictature pour les Centrafricains, c’est celle qui se vit loin des caméras. C’est celle des arrestations arbitraires, des détentions sans jugement, des disparitions forcées. C’est celle des opposants réduits au silence, des journalistes contraints à l’exil, des syndicalistes menacés, des étudiants matraqués. C’est celle d’un pouvoir qui ne tolère aucune contradiction, aucune critique, aucune alternative. « Le terrorisme, les trafics et les groupes armés prospèrent dans les zones que l’État ne contrôle plus », a-t-il reconnu devant l’ONU. Mais ces zones que l’État ne contrôle plus, c’est lui qui les a abandonnées. C’est lui qui a préféré confier la sécurité du pays à des mercenaires plutôt que de reconstruire une armée nationale républicaine. C’est lui qui a laissé Wagner et Africa Corps régner sans partage sur des provinces entières, pillant l’or, les diamants, le bétail, terrorisant les populations. Et pendant que ces hommes sèment la terreur dans les villages, Touadéra, lui, se prélasse dans les salons dorés de New York.
articles.lede: Découvrez comment le régime de Touadéra camoufle derrière ses discours internationaux la dictature et le pillage imposés aux Centrafricains.

articles.title: New UN Report Investigates Attacks on Aid Workers During Sri Lanka’s Civil War
articles.description: A new report by the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, “I Died Many Times”; Attacks on Humanitarian Assistance in Sri Lanka, documents the numerous threats aid workers faced during the final years of Sri Lanka’s civil war with the separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.
paragraphs: On August 4, 2006, 17 Sri Lankan staff members of the Paris-based humanitarian organization Action Contre la Faim (Action Against Hunger) were summarily executed at their office in Muttur, Sri Lanka. Over 20 years later, this unresolved case is emblematic of attacks on humanitarian workers during the country’s brutal civil war that ended in 2009.

A new report by the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, “I Died Many Times”; Attacks on Humanitarian Assistance in Sri Lanka, documents the numerous threats aid workers faced during the final years of Sri Lanka’s civil war with the separatist Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam.

The report finds that the government purposefully shut down humanitarian space “as a slow, deliberate strangulation” that effectively cordoned civilians into government-held areas, preventing independent observers from witnessing war crimes by the warring parties. The report, which is the latest from the UN’s Sri Lanka Accountability Project to gather evidence of international crimes in Sri Lanka, also finds “that impunity has resulted not from isolated failures, but from mutually reinforcing practices that have repeatedly frustrated accountability.”

The UN identifies four causes of impunity. First, it notes the state’s denial of responsibility. Second, the persistent failure of domestic investigations and prosecutions to deliver accountability. Third, it documents threats to victims, witnesses, and experts and the lack of effective witness protection in Sri Lanka. Lastly, it notes the appointment of presidential commissions of inquiry by successive governments instead of pursuing effective prosecutions.
Sri Lanka’s 26-year civil war was marked by serious human rights abuses and war crimes by both sides. Despite numerous domestic, international, and UN investigations, there has been no justice.

While President Anura Kumara Dissanayake took office in September 2024 promising justice for past rights abuses, most victims remain without answers or accountability because of the government’s failure to bring legal and structural reforms, including the promised independent public prosecutor’s office. The government has also refused to accept the Sri Lanka Accountability Project, which was established by the UN Human Rights Council in 2021 to collect evidence of serious rights abuses for use in possible future trials. This report shows why the UN’s evidence collection in Sri Lanka is as important as ever.

Conditions of KSC Detention
articles.description: The Kosovo Specialist Chambers has received some questions in recent days about the conditions at the Detention Facilities in The Hague and in this regard would like to share some important information with the public.
paragraphs: The KSC Detention Facilities operate in strict accordance with the requirements of humane treatment and respect for human dignity. All conditions meet or exceed European and international standards, including the United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners and the European Prison Rules. All forms of discrimination are prohibited in the Detention Facilities.

The Rules of Detention were developed in consultation with the International Committee of the Red Cross, which independently inspects and monitors detention conditions. This means that the ICRC may carry out regular, unannounced, and independent inspections to examine the conditions of detention and ensure compliance with human rights, international law, and accepted standards of treatment.

Detainees in The Hague have daily access to fresh air and physical exercise. They can participate in sports, such as tennis and soccer, engage in hobbies and recreational activities, such as gardening and painting, and they can cook and share meals together and socialize. Detainees may attend religious services. They have access to writing materials and language lessons are provided. They also have access to radio and television programmes in Albanian, as well as books, magazines, and newspapers. The standards of health care in the Detention Facilities meet or exceed those that are generally available to citizens in the Netherlands.

When it comes to food, detainees receive three meals each day. Meals are varied, well-prepared, and satisfying in quality and quantity as regards standards of nutrition. In addition, detainees who wish to prepare meals themselves, may use the provided cooking facilities and may purchase, at their own expense, ingredients from an outside provider.

Detainees do not have access to cash within the Detention Facilities, rather there is a transparent system of credit in place wherein money can be added to a detainee’s account to pay for items from outside providers.

When it comes to family life, the system in place inside the Detention Facilities provides every detainee with reasonable means of maintaining family and other personal relationships, including regular contact with family and friends through telephone calls and correspondence, in addition to in-person and video visits every month. Every detainee has 10 days every month for visits with family and friends. Detainees have regular private visits with spouses and children outside the sight and hearing of detention officers.
In addition to monitoring by the ICRC, the conditions of detention are also independently monitored by the KSC Ombudsperson, who has conducted 12 inspections, most recently in October 2026.

Detainees can make a complaint at any time to the Chief Detention Officer, the Ombudsperson of the Specialist Chambers or the ICRC. If they feel unheard, a complaints procedure allows them to bring their complaint to the Registrar and, if they are not satisfied with the response of the Registrar, before a panel of judges.
articles.lede: The Kosovo Specialist Chambers has received some questions in recent days about the conditions at the Detention Facilities in The Hague and in this regard would like to share some important information with the public.

articles.title: Will Filipinos get to hear Duterte’s trial?
articles.description: The International Criminal Court (ICC) could open its courtroom to the public without making the proceedings intelligible to the people who have waited longest the trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte. Translating international justice begins with language.
paragraphs: This November 30, if a family in the city of Davao, in southern Philippines, is looking for former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte’s trial, they can go to the International Criminal Court (ICC)’s website and read the opening notice in Cebuano. It gives the start time of the audience and tells them where to watch it with a 30-minute delay. It does not say whether they can hear the opening statements in Cebuano or find a translation afterwards.

At a hearing on November 2, Paolina Massidda, one of the lawyers representing victims, asked whether they could deliver 15 to 20 minutes of their opening statement in Tagalog, another language spoken in the Philippines. Her point was not that the judges needed to hear Tagalog. It was that the people in the country wanted to hear how their own accounts were being put before the judges. Presiding judge Joanna Korner turned down the request. She pointed to the Court’s working languages, English and French, to cost and complexity, and to the fact that not all victims speak Tagalog. She said she would ask the registry about making a Tagalog translation or transcript available online.

Those are defensible reasons. But they are not an answer to the question Massidda raised. If Tagalog would leave some victims out, that is an argument for reaching people in more than one language. A family in Davao might prefer Cebuano. Others may prefer Filipino or English. The Court has already recognised such a difference in the material it publishes about the case. It should therefore tell people what it will do with the proceedings themselves.

There are three different things at stake here. Under the Rome Statute, the accused is entitled to competent interpretation and the translations necessary for a fair trial. That is a right, not a favour. Then there is the interpretation that allows witnesses to give evidence in a language they are comfortable using. Neither tells a viewer in the Philippines what language will be available on the public feed or what they will be able to read afterwards. Providing a way for the viewers to follow the trial need not come at the expense of a fair hearing.

We already know what can happen when the distinction gets lost. A false claim circulated on Facebook that witnesses had been banned from testifying in Tagalog and therefore wanted to go home. That wasn’t the decision. It concerned part of the opening statement of the victims’ lawyers, not the language witnesses could use on the stand. VERA Files did the work of factchecking it. But the false version was simpler to tell, and the first witness had not even been called.

Philippine journalists have been doing more than correcting falsehoods. In February, MindaNews published victims’ counsel Joel Butuyan’s opening statement from the confirmation hearing, giving readers a chance to see the argument for themselves. The independent Philippine Truth Commission has published updates in English, Tagalog and Cebuano. The ICC does not need to take over that work: it should just give local journalists and the civil society more material they could use and check.
articles.lede: The International Criminal Court (ICC) could open its courtroom to the public without making the proceedings intelligible to the people who have waited longest the trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte.

articles.title: Awful but Lawful? The relevance of IHL Compliance to Genocide Allegations in The Gambia v. Myanmar
articles.description: On 19 November, the International Court of Justice delivered its much-anticipated judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar Genocide case. One issue the Court considered in the case was the interplay betwe…
paragraphs: On 19 November, the International Court of Justice delivered its much-anticipated judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar Genocide case. One issue the Court considered in the case was the interplay between international humanitarian law (IHL) and the Genocide Convention. While this issue may appear to be a minor theoretical point addressed by the Court only briefly, it ultimately turns on a consequential and undertheorised question: whether compliance with IHL in armed conflicts can serve as a blanket argument to counter allegations of genocide. The question is also likely to be highly relevant in the South Africa v. Israel case, currently on the ICJ’s docket, where Israel refers to compliance with IHL in response to the allegations of genocide against it (see here and the relevant analysis here ).

This post examines how the Court has approached the relationship between IHL and the Genocide Convention in its recent judgment in The Gambia v. Myanmar, focusing on the relevance of IHL compliance to the underlying acts of genocide and the mental elements of genocide. In doing so, it first analyses the Court’s reasoning in Croatia v. Serbia Genocide case, the principal point of reference on the matter in the academic discourse and in The Gambia v. Myanmar. It then considers whether The Gambia v. Myanmar addressed questions left open by the earlier judgment. The analysis in this post is confined to State responsibility under the Genocide Convention, rather than individual criminal responsibility.

The Court has previously faced the interplay between IHL and the Genocide Convention in the Croatia v. Serbia Genocide case. There, it stated in general terms that “the [Genocide] Convention and international humanitarian law are two distinct bodies of rules, pursuing different aims”. It nevertheless acknowledged that “[i]n so far as both of these bodies of rules may be applicable in the context of a particular armed conflict, the rules of international humanitarian law might be relevant in order to decide whether the acts alleged by the Parties constitute genocide within the meaning of Article II of the Convention” (para 153, emphasis added).

The Court, however, did not specify the precise role that IHL might play in this assessment in the relevant part on the interplay between IHL and the Genocide Convention. In particular, it left open whether IHL could inform the determination of the underlying acts of genocide ( actus reus ), the mental element required for those acts ( dolus generalis, or the intention to commit the underlying prohibited acts) and/or the intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a protected group ( dolus specialis, or genocidal intent). However, the Court’s subsequent analysis in the case offers some clarifications.

In considering Croatia’s claim in the part of dolus specialis, the Court held that “of the 17 factors suggested by Croatia to establish the existence of a pattern of conduct revealing a genocidal intent”, one of the most important factors is “the fact that those attacks are said to have caused casualties and damage far in excess of what was justified by military necessity”.

articles.title: ICC: Promote, Protect International Justice
articles.description: Member countries of the International Criminal Court (ICC) should prioritize measures to promote and protect the court and those cooperating with it.
paragraphs: (The Hague) – Member countries of the International Criminal Court (ICC) should prioritize measures to promote and protect the court and those cooperating with it, Human Rights Watch said in a report released today. The 24-page report makes detailed recommendations for the annual session of the ICC’s Assembly of States Parties, which will convene in The Hague from November 30 to December 7, 2026.

This year’s session takes place as the court and the broader international justice system face unrelenting pressure from the United States. On October 9, the US government escalated its campaign to destroy the ICC “brick by brick” by imposing sanctions on the whole court under a February 2025 executive order. This followed the sanctioning of ICC judges and prosecutors, a United Nations human rights expert, and three leading Palestinian rights organizations. Yet, the ICC continues to advance its critical work for justice. The landmark trial of former Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte is scheduled to begin on November 30.

“The start of the Duterte trial at the same time as the annual ICC Assembly session should remind member countries of the court’s critical importance,” said Liz Evenson, international justice director at Human Rights Watch. “At the session, member countries should stand firmly by the court and not take steps that could curtail victims’ access to justice.”

In his October 9 announcement, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio stated the sanctions were aimed at shielding US nationals from investigation and prosecution at the ICC. The Trump administration has previously objected to the court’s investigation of Israeli nationals for their conduct in Palestine. The ICC has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant for serious crimes in Gaza.

After a China-Russia-US summit––at which the three countries’ leaders adopted a declaration that included expressing concern for state consent and the immunity of state officials, and that the ICC and other similar bodies should not “abuse their jurisdiction”––US President Donald Trump on November 20 remarked that Russian President Vladimir Putin “especially is not happy with” the ICC. Putin faces war crimes charges before the ICC for the unlawful deportation and forcible transfer of children from occupied areas of Ukraine to Russia.

The US government has pitched the court-wide sanctions as “structured ... to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address” its “concerns.” The authorization of certain transactions with the court for a six-month period, which otherwise would have been immediately affected by the court-wide sanctions, is an ultimatum to member countries to meet the US government’s demands; but these demands effectively allow the Trump administration to determine whom the court can prosecute, Human Rights Watch said.

In the lead-up to the Assembly session, media reports referred to concerning proposals by some countries to meet US demands, including curbing the court’s jurisdiction over nationals of nonmember countries or exempting heads of state from the court’s reach. Offering the US government solutions that would hollow out the court’s mandate and guarantee impunity for certain powerful individuals would severely undermine the legitimacy and credibility of the ICC and the international justice system, Human Rights Watch said.
articles.lede: Member countries of the International Criminal Court (ICC) should prioritize measures to promote and protect the court and those cooperating with it.

articles.title: Fact-finding in the age of distrust: the continued relevance of the IHFFC
articles.description: In an era of contested facts and declining trust, the IHFFC could play a vital role in restoring respect for international humanitarian law.
paragraphs: At a time when allegations of serious violations of international humanitarian law (IHL) are increasingly contested, establishing the facts independently and impartially seems more important yet difficult than ever. Political divisions and declining trust in international institutions have made credible fact-finding particularly challenging. Yet the international community does not need to start from scratch. More than three decades ago, states established the International Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission (IHFFC), a permanent, independent mechanism to inquire into alleged serious violations of IHL and facilitate the restoration of respect for the law. The Commission has demonstrated its ability to operate, yet it is rarely used. The challenge is therefore not to create new mechanisms, but to make better use of those already existing, particularly those rooted in international treaties.

In this post, Cristina Azzarello, Humanitarian Affairs and Migration Adviser at the Permanent Mission of Italy in Geneva, examines the continued relevance of the IHFFC at a time when compliance with IHL is under considerable strain. Rather than questioning whether the Commission can operate, she considers what its experience tells us about its potential and how it might play a more significant role in the efforts to strengthen respect for IHL.

A hospital has been hit during an armed conflict. Contradictory reports emerge about who was responsible and what happened. Reports, photos and videos spread rapidly. Distinguishing reliable evidence from misinformation or manipulated content can be difficult. Under these conditions, independent and impartial fact-finding could be essential to establish what happened, prevent further violations and restore respect for international humanitarian law (IHL).

The International Humanitarian Fact-Finding Commission (IHFFC) was established under Article 90 of Additional Protocol I of 1977 (API) to the Geneva Conventions of 1949 to enquire into any facts alleged to constitute grave breaches or other serious violations of IHL and to facilitate, through its good offices, the restoration of an attitude of respect for the provisions of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and API. To date, 78 states have formally recognized the Commission’s competence under Article 90, while its good offices have been invoked on only two occasions, in 2017 and 2024. It is striking that the IHFFC has been used so rarely. Unlike a court or criminal tribunal, its purpose is not to look into accountability, determine criminal responsibility or draw legal conclusions about whether a certain conduct constitutes an IHL violation, but to establish the facts independently and impartially and to reinforce the credibility of mechanisms designed to uphold IHL. [1]

Past practice has shown that it is no longer a body waiting to be activated. Yet, the IHFFC has still been called upon in a limited number of cases and the question is what can be done to further encourage its use.
articles.lede: In an era of contested facts and declining trust, the IHFFC could play a vital role in restoring respect for international humanitarian law.

Indonesia: One year after devastating Aceh floods, communities face renewed flood risk as recovery stalls
articles.description: One year after catastrophic floods and landslides devastated Indonesia’s Aceh province, many survivors remain without adequate housing, continue to struggle to access promised support and now face renewed flood risks from this year’s rainy season, Amnesty International said in new research published today. Amnesty’s briefing, A Continuing Crisis, found that many communities affected by the…
paragraphs: Amnesty’s briefing, A Continuing Crisis, found that many communities affected by the November 2025 disaster are still living with the consequences of inadequate response and recovery efforts. Many families remain in temporary shelters, damaged homes and makeshift accommodation, while reconstruction has progressed slowly and many survivors remain uncertain about what support they are entitled to receive.

“For the survivors in Aceh, this disaster did not end when the floodwaters receded. A year later, many families are still waiting for the housing and support they were promised by the Indonesian authorities,” said Montse Ferrer, Co-Regional Director at Amnesty International.

“But not only has this crisis been allowed to continue; it has the potential to get worse. The government’s unforgivably inept response to the floods of 2025 has now left people in Aceh facing another rainy season while key recovery work from the last disaster remains unfinished.”

In late November 2025, exceptionally heavy rainfall associated with Tropical Cyclone Senyar triggered floods, flash floods and landslides across Aceh and neighbouring provinces of North Sumatra and West Sumatra. The disaster affected 53 districts and cities, killed 1,204 people and displaced more than 880,000.
“I have lived through four crises – the Aceh conflict, the tsunami, Covid and these floods. Out of them all, I feel this is the worst.”

Amnesty International researchers visited more than 40 villages and spoke to 35 people across three of the worst-affected regencies in Aceh and found widespread evidence that reconstruction and mitigation for future floods remains incomplete. Researchers observed damaged homes, destroyed agricultural land, unrepaired infrastructure and communities continuing to rely on temporary water sources.
One affected resident told Ammesty: “I have lived through four crises – the Aceh conflict, the tsunami, Covid and these floods. Out of them all, I feel this is the worst.”

Indonesia’s government announced multibillion-dollar plans for rehabilitation and reconstruction across the affected provinces. Yet official figures show that only 649 of the 34,777 permanent homes required in Aceh had been completed by September 2026.

Across the villages visited by researchers, Amnesty International did not encounter a single family whose replacement home had been completed. Many survivors remained in temporary housing or accommodation provided by relatives and friends. Most had no information about when permanent housing would become available.
articles.lede: Amnesty’s briefing, A Continuing Crisis, found that many communities affected by the November 2025 disaster are still living with the consequences of inadequate response and recovery efforts.

Centrafrique: comment Touadéra et Abazene instrumentalisent la justice pour broyer l’opposition et installer leur dictature
articles.description: Écouter l'articleTélécharger Le masque est définitivement tombé. Lors de son discours de couronnement du 30 mars dernier, Faustin-Archange Touadéra
paragraphs: Le masque est définitivement tombé. Lors de son discours de couronnement du 30 mars dernier, Faustin-Archange Touadéra avait jeté les bases d’une répression d’un nouveau genre en ordonnant explicitement la traque de tous ceux qui utilisent les réseaux sociaux pour contester son troisième mandat. En qualifiant les opposants et certains pays de « relais clandestins » et d’« ennemis de la République », le chef de l’État appelait ses partisans à la délation généralisée.

Le mode opératoire de cette inquisition numérique est désormais clair et bien rodé: le régime dresse des listes de citoyens à abattre politiquement, les remet à ses activistes inféodés pour diffusion via des publications Facebook, des messages vocaux ou des vidéos en direct, avant que le ministre d’État Arnaud Djoubaye Abazene n’en informe Touadéra et ses partenaires russes afin de mettre le parquet en mouvement.
C’est précisément ce rouage machiavélique qui vient d’être activé par une publication téléguidée proche du pouvoir, plongeant le pays dans une parodie judiciaire sans précédent.

Les déclarations du 30 mars n’étaient donc pas de simples effets de tribune. Quelques semaines plus tard, elles trouvent déjà une traduction concrète dans le fonctionnement même des institutions censées garantir l’État de droit. Le dernier communiqué du parquet de Bangui en fournit une illustration saisissante.

C’est dans une lecture laborieuse diffusée sur les ondes de la Radio-Télévision Centrafricaine que le premier substitut spécialisé près le parquet de Bangui, Guy Félix Yaguemet, a ouvert les hostilités. Dans un communiqué par lequel il dit vouloir informer l’opinion nationale, Guy Félix Yaguemet a annoncé l’ouverture d’une enquête judiciaire sur la base d’un simple écrit publié sur les réseaux sociaux par une voix zélée du régime en France. Un procédé grotesque qui démontre que la justice centrafricaine n’est plus qu’une chambre d’enregistrement des dénonciations calomnieuses du parti au pouvoir.

Mais au-delà des annonces spectaculaires et des effets de communication, plusieurs incohérences majeures apparaissent dès que l’on examine le dossier de plus près. La plus frappante concerne l’entourage même des personnes citées dans cette affaire.

Pourtant, cette mise en scène se heurte immédiatement à une autre contradiction flagrante et historique. Ce complot présumé implique nommément Danzoumi Yalo. Comment expliquer que son frère, Sani Yalo, pilier du renseignement informel et parrain financier du régime, n’ait rien vu, rien entendu et rien révélé de cette affaire?

Ce parfum de complicité ou d’incompétence rappelle étrangement l’épisode du coup d’État manqué en Guinée équatoriale. À l’époque, un autre frère cadet de Sani Yalo, Dada Yalo, s’était engagé comme commando dans l’opération avant d’être arrêté, sans que Sani Yalo n’ait jamais rien dénoncé. Pire encore, Sani Yalo lui-même a déjà été nommément cité et entendu par la justice centrafricaine dans un précédent projet de coup d’État impliquant directement Karim Meckassoua. Le voilà donc, de près ou de loin, indirectement connecté à une nouvelle affaire de déstabilisation.
articles.lede: Le masque est définitivement tombé.

articles.title: Germany: Funding Cuts Threaten Anti-Discrimination Efforts
articles.description: The German government’s decision to discontinue funding for dozens of civil society projects, following budget cuts, undermines the country’s efforts to address racism, discrimination and antisemitism and protect human rights, Human Rights Watch said today. The German government and Bundestag should release further funds to guarantee the continuation of dozens of essential civil society projects. The Bundestag is due to vote on the federal budget on November 27, 2026.
paragraphs: (Berlin, November 26, 2026) – The German government’s decision to discontinue funding for dozens of civil society projects, following budget cuts, undermines Germany’s efforts to address racism, discrimination, and antisemitism and protect human rights, Human Rights Watch said today. The German government and Bundestag should release further funds to guarantee the continuation of dozens of essential civil society projects. The Bundestag is due to vote on the federal budget on November 27, 2026.

“The German government’s cuts undermine critical civil society work and networks that directly protect human rights and combat the threats from the far-right,” said Almaz Teffera, senior Europe researcher at Human Rights Watch. “The German government and Bundestag should remedy the cuts in the federal budget by providing funds to save trusted anti-discrimination and anti-extremism work that directly protects and empowers people at this critical time.”

On November 12, the Bundestag’s budgetary committee approved the government’s proposed cuts of about €20 million to the federal civil society democracy fund, “Live Democracy!” (“Demokratie Leben!”). On November 13, the government sent funding rejections to dozens of trusted civil society projects that monitor and document discrimination and hate crimes, foster civic engagement and education, and support victims and those at risk amid alarming levels of hate crimes.

In March, the government announced that it intended to restructure the Live Democracy! program and required all funded initiatives and projects to reapply. The government introduced new criteria and objectives, which the education and family affairs minister, Karin Prien, said would mean funded initiatives “ reach the silent majority [in society], which is in danger of turning away from democracy .” The cuts undermine the work of civil society groups that advocate for human rights, diversity, and democracy.

Live Democracy! began in 2015 as a response to racially motivated right-wing extremist terror cases in Germany in the early 2000s and subsequent institutional failures. The program had supported civil society groups, initiatives, and structures to push back against extremism, racism, and antisemitism, aiming to strengthen Germany’s democracy, promote diversity, and prevent extremism. Prien removed the goal of promoting diversity, claiming that it was “ not a sufficient funding objective” on its own. Projects on racism, antisemitism, or other hostility against a group fall under the category of preventing extremism, with a restricted list of potentially fundable activities.

According to media reports, the government invited only 150 out of 1,200 applicants who expressed interest in funding to submit a full funding application. The program had previously funded about 600 projects. Several applications for projects on anti-Black and anti-Muslim racism as well as antisemitism and right-wing extremism received partial or full rejections.

Previous funding from Live Democracy! was used by civil society groups like CLAIM, which works to combat anti-Muslim racism and hatred, to partially finance vital civil society monitoring and documentation infrastructure to track anti-Muslim discrimination and hate incidents. The group said that discontinuing their funding puts Muslim people in Germany at risk at a time when anti-Muslim incidents are at a record high.
articles.lede: The German government’s decision to discontinue funding for dozens of civil society projects, following budget cuts, undermines the country’s efforts to address racism, discrimination and antisemitism and protect human…

articles.title: Nepal: Predatory Lending Abuses Exacerbated by Conflict in the Gulf
articles.description: Authorities in Nepal should hold illegal moneylenders accountable for abuses against borrowers, including unlawful land dispossession, arbitrary eviction, threats and acts of violence, and sexual exploitation.
paragraphs: (Tokyo) – Authorities in Nepal should hold illegal moneylenders accountable for abuses against borrowers, including unlawful land dispossession, arbitrary eviction, threats and acts of violence, and sexual exploitation, Human Rights Watch said today. Conflicts in the Gulf region, where many Nepalis are migrant workers facing exorbitant recruitment fees, have made more people vulnerable to extortion by illegal lenders.

“Despite government commitments to protect borrowers, illegal practices are rife in Nepal’s informal credit sector, leaving those with the fewest resources dependent on moneylenders who can take everything they own,” said Meenakshi Ganguly, Asia deputy director at Human Rights Watch. “The government of Prime Minister Balendra Shah should carry out the government’s commitments to ensure that the law against fraudulent and abusive lending is consistently enforced.”

Human Rights Watch interviewed 18 borrowers, as well as local government officials, lawyers, and activists from six districts in the Terai region where informal money lending is rampant, reviewed government reports, and examined over 50 cases in Nawalparasi district.

Human Rights Watch found that many families are struggling with unmanageable debt particularly as migrant workers in the Gulf States during 2026 have faced reduced incomes or involuntary travel delays ahead of starting jobs due to the conflict between the US, Israel, and Iran. War-induced disruption amplified pre-existing abuses, including reliance on unauthorized individual agents and unreasonable recruitment fees. Human Rights Watch previously found that companies in Gulf states play a critical role in driving these illegal costs by refusing to cover costs and fees to recruiters that they know will be borne by workers.

Government investigations have shown that, under Nepal’s informal credit practices, a borrower signs or thumbprints an unsecured personal loan contract, known locally as kapali tamasuk, which can falsely list a principal amount three to ten times more than the cash received. These loans, known as meter byaj, in some cases compound at annual rates ranging from 36 percent to 60 percent or more, compared with less than 10 percent charged by banks.

As low-income households that had relied on remittances disrupted by the war have shifted their limited resources toward expenses for food, fuel, and healthcare, they have been increasingly unable to repay their loans, leading to a surge in defaults. In response, some moneylenders are forcing evictions or land transfers, including through violence, in the worst cases tying people into generational debt. Nepal authorities are not pushing for effective long term solutions beyond encouraging and facilitating debtors and creditors to enter pre-court settlements.

Following the outbreak of conflict in the Persian Gulf, in March 2026, the Nepal government suspended both institutional and individual labor permits to protect its citizens, including to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, and Kuwait, with an estimated 2,000 Nepalis denied labor permits daily. Thousands were stopped from travelling at the international airport despite possessing valid medical clearances, verified visas, and binding employment contracts, while administrative delays also led foreign firms to cancel labor contracts. However, the authorities failed to step in to protect aspiring migrant laborers who still had to service their high interest meter byaj loans, leaving them exposed to violent enforcement by loan sharks.
articles.lede: Authorities in Nepal should hold illegal moneylenders accountable for abuses against borrowers, including unlawful land dispossession, arbitrary eviction, threats and acts of violence, and sexual exploitation.

articles.title: drame de Zamboye: pour Rosine Zalang, Qui s’occupe des enfants orphelins? Qui s’occupe des veuves? après les condoléances, les familles des victimes restent face aux conséquences du drame
articles.description: Écouter l'articleTélécharger Rosine Zalang, coordinatrice de l’association Jeunesse en marche pour le développement en Centrafrique, estime que la
paragraphs: Rosine Zalang, coordinatrice de l’association Jeunesse en marche pour le développement en Centrafrique, estime que la prise en charge des victimes du drame de Zamboye ne peut pas s’arrêter aux condoléances et à l’assistance d’urgence. Pour elle, les familles qui ont perdu leurs principaux soutiens doivent bénéficier de mesures concrètes et durables.
Lors de l’émission « Patara » consacrée au drame de Zamboye sur Radio Ndeke Luka, Rosine Zalang a placé la protection de la vie humaine au centre de son intervention.
Elle a d’abord rejeté les explications qui tendent à présenter l’exploitation anarchique du site comme une conséquence inévitable de la pauvreté ou de la recherche de revenus.
« La vie, la vie qui est sacrée, l’homme qui est sacré n’est pas au centre de préoccupation de l’intérêt économique ou bien de l’intérêt politique de notre pays », affirme Rosine Zalang.
À lire aussi: Touadera et Zingas, les bras cassés de la septième république, regardez! Le CEG de Mboula risque de fermer ses portes. Pensez-vous à l’avenir de ces enfants?

Pour la responsable associative, les difficultés économiques des populations ne peuvent pas justifier leur exposition à des risques mortels. Elle estime que la protection des travailleurs et des personnes présentes sur les sites miniers doit rester une responsabilité prioritaire des autorités.
À lire aussi: Assassinats nocturnes, enlèvements et cherté de la vie: Abakar Sabone décrit le quotidien des Centrafricains

Rosine Zalang revient notamment sur l’argument selon lequel les populations seraient retournées dans les excavations pour récupérer des résidus d’or ou de gravier. Pour elle, cette situation ne dispense pas les responsables du secteur minier de leurs obligations en matière de sécurité.
« Il est important de mettre d’abord a priori la valeur humaine des Centrafricains et en particulier la jeunesse », déclare-t-elle.

La coordinatrice de Jeunesse en marche pour le développement en Centrafrique insiste sur le fait que la prévention doit intervenir avant les catastrophes. Elle dénonce une pratique consistant à attendre qu’un drame survienne avant d’ouvrir des enquêtes ou de rechercher les responsabilités.

GC IV Commentary Series – Protecting Powers: From Failure to Function
articles.description: The evolution of the protecting power system since 1949 highlights a tension between humanitarian considerations and State sovereignty.
paragraphs: Editors’ note: The following series considers ICRC’s 2025 updated Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention. Rosa-Lena Lauterbach, Liisi Adamson, and Sean Watts’s introduction to the series is available here.

The optimism of Dr. Jean Pictet’s original Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention (1958 Commentary) concerning Article 9 of that Convention is impossible to ignore. Based on their shared experiences of recent armed conflicts, States made the protecting power system the central mechanism for ensuring that the parties to an international armed conflict complied with their humanitarian obligations towards persons protected by the 1949 Geneva Conventions. In so doing the Diplomatic Conference had successfully reconciled claims of national sovereignty with humanitarian considerations and made a “huge advance” in the development of international humanitarian law (p. 91).

However, States’ practice since 1958 undermines the optimism of the 1958 Commentary. Instead of States embracing a system of compulsory supervision, the appointment by a State of a protecting power has been the rarest exception rather than the rule. This has led one commentator to question whether “the protecting powers regime has proved perhaps the signal failure of the 1949 Conventions”?

It is against this backdrop that readers must assess the 2025 Commentary on the Fourth Geneva Convention (2025 Commentary ). The product of extensive collaboration and consultation over several years, the key challenge for the 2025 Commentary in respect of the protecting power system has been to examine State practice since the adoption of the Geneva Conventions and make sense of why it did not develop as its proponents expected. It addresses this development in two insightful ways. First, it develops the notion that a protecting power may operate under a dual mandate of diplomatic law (a “Vienna mandate”) and international humanitarian law (a “Geneva Mandate”) (2025 Commentary, para. 1260 ). Second, rather than avoiding the challenge, the 2025 Commentary directly acknowledges that States have chosen to interpret the ostensible requirement to appoint a protecting power as optional rather than mandatory ( para. 1238 ). Stressing the imperative of a functional approach, the 2025 Commentary consequently emphasises that a failure to appoint a protecting power does not relieve the parties to an international armed conflict of the requirement to facilitate the supervision of their compliance with the applicable provisions of Geneva Convention IV (GC IV) (para. 1340 ).
Before turning to consider these factors in more detail, it is first necessary to briefly chart the development of the protecting powers system.

The protecting power system is rooted in diplomatic practice. States have routinely exercised the right of legation since at least the seventeenth century, even though there is no international legal obligation to do so (see, e.g., Satow, p. 175-80). In exercise of that right, it has become commonplace for a State to send diplomatic agents, and in some cases establish permanent missions or embassies, for the purpose of protecting its own national interests in another State.
articles.lede: The evolution of the protecting power system since 1949 highlights a tension between humanitarian considerations and State sovereignty.

Transposition of the European due diligence: French law cannot backtrack
articles.description: In February 2026, the European Union adopted a legislative package known as “Omnibus I”, amending the European Directive on corporate due (…)
paragraphs: In February 2026, the European Union adopted a legislative package known as “Omnibus I”, amending the European Directive on corporate due diligence (CSDDD). Whilst France is due to transpose it by July 2028, member organisations of the Citizens’ Forum for Economic Justice asked Sophie Robin-Olivier, a lecturer at the Law School of Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne University, to analyse what this directive requires of the French legislature.

Paris, 25 November 2026. This directive, adopted in 2024 and aimed at protecting human rights and the environment from harm caused by businesses, has not yet been transposed into French law. Consequently, in this regard, the Act of 27 March 2017 on the due diligence of parent companies and contracting entities applies in France.

Professor Robin-Olivier’s conclusions are clear: transposition cannot be used as a justification for reducing the protection of human rights, social rights, the environment and the climate provided by the 2017 Act and its case law, including on points covered by full harmonisation. Wherever French law offers greater protection, it must be preserved.
Transposition cannot justify a reduction in the level of protection guaranteed by national law in relation to human rights, labour rights, social rights, and environmental and climate protection.
Unlike other directives, the text does not refer to a ‘general’ level of protection. Any reduction is therefore prohibited, even if it is modest or compensated for elsewhere.
The level of protection is assessed in the light of the law and the case law which has clarified its scope (e.g. judgments handed down in the La Poste case).
Omnibus I introduced the possibility of " adapting " the existing duty of care in order to ‘align’ it with the CSDDD. However, " aligning " does not mean " backtracking ".

Alignment merely allows for the amendment of provisions that do not enhance the protection of human rights and the environment and relate solely to differences in implementation across States (e.g. threshold criteria; replacement of the " established commercial relationship " with the European concept of " business partner ").
Full harmonisation does not take precedence over the principle of non-regression (Article 4)

The full harmonisation provided for by the Directive in respect of certain provisions applies " without prejudice " to the principle of non-regression and is therefore only required if it does not result in regression.
articles.lede: In February 2026, the European Union adopted a legislative package known as “Omnibus I”, amending the European Directive on corporate due (…)

articles.title: Israel / Occupied Palestinian Territory: Travel ban imposed on Shawan Jabarin, General Director of Al-Haq
articles.description: ISR 002 / 1126 / OBS 059 Travel ban / Administrative harassment / Restrictions on freedom of movement Israel / Occupied Palestinian Territory 25 (…)
paragraphs: The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Israel / Occupied Palestinian Territory.
The Observatory has been informed about the imposition of a travel ban on Mr Shawan Jabarin, General Director of the Palestinian human rights organisation Al-Haq and former Secretary General of FIDH.

On 13 November 2026, Israeli forces kept Mr Shawan Jabarin’s passport at the Allenby (Al-Karameh) Bridge, preventing him from leaving the Occupied Palestinian Territory to travel to Jordan. He was made to wait for approximately three hours at the border crossing. During this time, he was questioned about the purpose of his journey before being informed that he was subject to a travel ban. His passport was subsequently returned to him that same day and no explanation or legal grounds for the decision were provided to him.

The Observatory recalls that this is not the first time that Mr Jabarin has been subjected to travel restrictions in connection with his work as General Director of Al-Haq. In 2006, the Israeli authorities imposed a travel ban on him based on secret evidence, preventing him from carrying out his advocacy activities abroad. In 2009, the Israeli Supreme Court also denied him permission to travel to the Netherlands to receive the Geuzenpenning Prize on behalf of Al-Haq. The ban remained in force for six years, until it was temporarily lifted in 2012, subject to conditions.

Mr Jabarin has also faced threats in connection with his human rights activities. In August 2022, he received a threatening telephone call from the Israeli security service Shin Bet, warning him of possible arrest, imprisonment and other personal consequences if he continued his advocacy work and that of Al-Haq. In 2016, he had also received death threats from an anonymous caller, in the context of Al-Haq’s advocacy efforts to seek accountability for alleged war crimes committed in Palestine before the International Criminal Court (ICC).

The Observatory is concerned that this arbitrary travel ban constitutes an act of retaliation against Mr Jabarin for his legitimate human rights work and forms part of a broader pattern of restrictions and intimidation targeting Palestinian human rights defenders and civil society organisations. The latest travel ban must also be viewed against the backdrop of increasing pressure on Palestinian human rights organisations. In September 2025, the United States imposed sanctions on Al-Haq, the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights and the Al Mezan Center for Human Rights, citing their cooperation with the ICC. These sanctions have severely endangered the organisations’ operations, including by restricting their access to funding and undermining their ability to document violations.

articles.title: Transposition du devoir de vigilance européen: la loi française ne peut pas reculer
articles.description: En février 2026, l’Union européenne a adopté un paquet législatif dit “Omnibus I” modifiant la directive européenne sur le devoir de vigilance des (…)
paragraphs: En février 2026, l’Union européenne a adopté un paquet législatif dit “Omnibus I” modifiant la directive européenne sur le devoir de vigilance des entreprises (CSDDD). Alors que la France doit la transposer d’ici juillet 2028, les associations membres du Forum citoyen pour la justice économique ont demandé à Sophie Robin-Olivier, professeure à l’École de droit de l’université Paris 1 Panthéon-Sorbonne, d’analyser ce que cette directive impose au législateur français.

Paris, 25 novembre 2026. Cette directive, adoptée en 2024 et visant à protéger les droits humains et l’environnement des dommages causés par les entreprises, n’a pas encore fait l’objet d’une transposition en droit français. De ce fait, en la matière, c’est la loi du 27 mars 2017 relative au devoir de vigilance des sociétés mères et des entreprises donneuses d’ordre qui s’applique en France.

Les conclusions de Pr. Robin-Olivier sont claires: la transposition ne peut pas servir de motif pour réduire la protection des droits humains, des droits sociaux, de l’environnement et du climat assurée par la loi de 2017 et sa jurisprudence, y compris sur des points couverts par l’harmonisation complète. Partout où le droit français est plus protecteur, il doit être préservé.

La transposition ne peut pas justifier une réduction du niveau de protection garanti par le droit national en matière de droits humains, droits du travail, droits sociaux, protection de l’environnement et du climat.
Contrairement à d’autres directives, le texte ne se réfère pas à un niveau de protection « général ». Toute réduction est donc interdite, même modeste ou compensée ailleurs.
Le niveau de protection s’apprécie au regard de la loi et de la jurisprudence qui en a précisé la portée (par ex. décisions rendues dans l’affaire La Poste).
L’Omnibus I a introduit la possibilité d’ « adapter » le devoir de vigilance existant pour l’« aligner » sur la CSDDD. Mais « aligner » ne signifie pas « reculer ».

L’alignement permet seulement de modifier des dispositions qui n’améliorent pas la protection des droits humains et de l’environnement et tiennent uniquement à des modalités différentes selon les États (ex. critères de seuils; remplacement de la « relation commerciale établie » par la notion européenne de « partenaire commercial »).
L’harmonisation complète prévue par la directive pour certaines de ses dispositions s’applique « sans préjudice » de la non-régression et ne s’impose donc que si elle n’entraîne pas de régression.
La CSDDD interdit seulement aux États d’« introduire » des dispositions divergentes, et non de les « maintenir ».
articles.lede: En février 2026, l’Union européenne a adopté un paquet législatif dit “Omnibus I” modifiant la directive européenne sur le devoir de vigilance des (…)
